detail.abstract: Shame is usually described as a social emotion, a response to being seen and found wanting. This paper argues that account is incomplete. Drawing on lateral habenula (LHb) physiology, insular interoception, and the evolutionary history of valence itself, it makes four claims. First, shame is precognitive: the LHb renders its verdict before conscious awareness can weigh in, so the self who feels ashamed did not decide to feel that way and cannot simply reason its way out. Second, recognizing this fact is itself a small shame event, because it strips the conscious self of an authorship it assumes it has-a likely reason the mechanics of shame have resisted plain description for so long. Third, the insula is the organ that converts the habenula's binary verdict into felt experience, turning an external stimulus into an internal, inescapable sense of wrongness. Fourth, because valence predates social life by billions of years, shame does not require a witness; private failure, with no one watching, can trigger the full mechanism. The paper closes by tracing how early coregulation and oxytocin raise the habenular threshold over development, and what this means for treatment.

title: Noise, Ghosts, and Adverse Selection: Market Microstructure in Decentralized Sports Prediction Markets

detail.title: Noise, Ghosts, and Adverse Selection: Market Microstructure in Decentralized Sports Prediction Markets
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the tick-level microstructure of decentralized prediction markets, focusing on how they process discrete information shocks compared to centralized data feeds. Using a millisecond-resolution dual-feed dataset of order book states and API match updates across 25 T20 cricket matches (16 IPL, 9 T20 Blast), three phenomena are documented. First, an average 6.63-second information latency gap exists between on-chain execution by informed traders and public API registration. Second, spoofing activity ("Ghost Orders") scales dynamically with ambient liquidity: 58 confirmed instances in the high-liquidity IPL sample, zero in the low-liquidity T20 Blast sample, with a mean flash-to-pull cycle of 116.4 milliseconds, well below the threshold of human reaction time. Third, Ghost Order frequency in the 10 seconds preceding a wicket is statistically indistinguishable from the quiet-play baseline (2 observed vs. 0.72 expected; upper-tail p = 0.1628, cumulative P(X<=2) = 0.9632). These findings provide empirical validation of Glosten-Milgrom adverse selection theory in a decentralized setting, demonstrating that market manipulation operates as a structural background activity that ceases precisely when the probability of facing an informed counterparty is highest.

title: Bargaining Power in the Market for Ideas
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania and Shanghai Jiao Tong University (SJTU) - Antai College of Economics and Management

detail.title: Bargaining Power in the Market for Ideas
detail.abstract: We study the division of total surplus between buyers and sellers in patent transactions and its impact on the development of ideas. Using comprehensive data on U.S. patent transactions from 1975 to 2012, we estimate gains from trade for both parties based on how their stock prices react to patent transaction news. Additionally, we quantify bargaining shares as the proportion of their gains from trade within the total surplus. We find that firms' bargaining shares are heterogeneous and proportional to their size relative to their counterparties, starkly contrasting to the conventional assumption of homogeneous and fixed bargaining shares in the literature. We further show that the relationship between relative size and bargaining share is stronger among firms with weaker corporate governance. To study the implications of these findings, we develop a model with size-dependent bargaining power in the patent market. Our analysis shows that the substantial bargaining power of large firms diminishes the incentive for innovation among smaller firms.

title: Trade Diversification and Food Price Volatility

detail.title: Trade Diversification and Food Price Volatility
detail.abstract: Recent shortages and price volatility have exposed vulnerabilities in international agri-food value chains. This paper develops a new framework for measuring trade diversification based on Hill numbers, which capture both the extensive and intensive margin of trade connections. Using HS6-level bilateral data for 188 countries from 2000 to 2022, I first document global patterns of diversification and concentration across agri-food sectors. The descriptive evidence shows that most countries trade with many partners in principle, yet effectively rely on only a few, especially for grains and oilseeds. I then estimate the effect of import and export diversification on within-year food price volatility using a shift-share instrumental-variable design that exploits exogenous foreign sector-level shocks weighted by lagged bilateral trade exposure. The empirical results show that more balanced and diversified import portfolios are strongly associated with lower food price volatility, whereas export diversification plays a more limited role. Policies encouraging diversification can reduce food price volatility but involve trade-offs between efficiency from international specialization and resilience of the input-output network.

title: Yield Curve Prediction with Machine Learning: Forecasting Approaches and the Role of Macroeconomic Predictors

detail.title: Yield Curve Prediction with Machine Learning: Forecasting Approaches and the Role of Macroeconomic Predictors
detail.abstract: This paper compares direct-yield and factor-based approaches to U.S. Treasury yield curve forecasting using a common high-dimensional macroeconomic information set. Forecasts are evaluated on monthly zero-coupon yields over the 2015-2025 out-of-sample period. Gains over the random walk are concentrated at short maturities and in slope forecasts, and decline with the forecast horizon. Direct-yield models perform best for slope forecasts and are relatively stronger at short horizons, while factor-based models become more competitive at longer horizons. Macroeconomic predictors provide clear incremental predictive power, strongest for slope related movements. A trading simulation reinforces that macro-augmented models perform best in slope trades. The simulation also highlights a gap between statistical and economic performance, as the random walk is a strong benchmark under statistical loss but performs poorly as a trading signal.

title: Europe’s Climate Ambition Under Scrutiny: Evidence from Deep Learning Emission Projections
affiliations: Polytechnic University of Milan, RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment, RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment and Polytechnic University of Milan

detail.title: Europe’s Climate Ambition Under Scrutiny: Evidence from Deep Learning Emission Projections
detail.abstract: The European Union has committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions 55\% below 1990 levels by 2030, but whether current trends are compatible with this ambition remains uncertain. We apply deep learning to high-resolution socioeconomic and sectoral data across EU27 member states till 2023 to project sectoral CO$_2$ trajectories under current trends, extrapolating observed sectoral momentum without assuming changes in the pace or effectiveness of the policy environment beyond what is already reflected in historical data. We project that EU27 emissions will exceed the 2030 target by 35\% (620 Mt CO$_2$ shortfall), with only a small minority of countries on trajectories consistent with the bloc's commitments. While the Power sector achieves target-consistent reductions driven by the renewable transition, Mobility shows minimal progress and accounts for over a third of total emissions by 2030, reflecting a structural inertia across member states rather than geographically concentrated lag. Our findings indicate that substantial additional intervention is required to close Europe's ambition-implementation gap, and call for establishing up-to-date energy information in Europe.

title: Configurations of Internal and External Barriers to GSCM Adoption in Egyptian Petrochemicals: A Synthetic SEM-fsQCA Study

detail.title: Configurations of Internal and External Barriers to GSCM Adoption in Egyptian Petrochemicals: A Synthetic SEM-fsQCA Study

keywords: Green Supply Chain Adoption Barriers in Egypt's Petrochemical Sector

detail.abstract: This completed study examines green supply chain adoption barriers in Egypt's petrochemical sector through synthetic latent-variable modeling and fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis. The analysis is anchored in a bounded fifteensource Egyptian and MENA supply chain corpus and uses only those references. The net-effect model explained 32.5% of synthetic adoption variance. Internal, external, and human barriers were negative, while digital readiness, supplier support, and regulatory clarity were positive. The strongest illustrative configuration achieved consistency of 0.60. The study contributes a reproducible analytical framework, explicit assumptions, numerical or coded results, tables, and code-generated figures. It does not claim that generated observations are measurements of Egyptian organizations. Its valid contribution is method validation, scenario comparison, decision sensitivity, or bounded content analysis. The paper concludes with managerial, policy, and research implications and specifies the evidence needed for external validation.

title: A Unified Inferential Framework for Dynamic Asset Pricing with Time-varying Risk Exposures
affiliations: Nankai University, Southeast University and Nankai University

detail.title: A Unified Inferential Framework for Dynamic Asset Pricing with Time-varying Risk Exposures
detail.abstract: Testing whether asset pricing alphas are jointly zero is a central problem in empirical finance, particularly when the number of assets is large and factor loadings vary over time. We develop a new class of high-dimensional alpha tests for such models by combining spline-based varying-coefficient estimation with finite-even-order L q-norm statistics. After removing the nonparametric nuisance component by B-spline projection, we construct studentized statistics for average alphas and propose L 2 , L 4 , L 6 , max-type, and Cauchy combination tests. We establish the asymptotic validity of the proposed procedures under the null and show that higher-order L q statistics are more effective against sparse alternatives with stronger signals, while the combination test improves adaptivity across different sparsity regimes. Simulations show good finite-sample size and power performance, and an empirical application illustrates the usefulness of the proposed methods for detecting pricing anomalies under time-varying risk exposures.

title: The Readiness Option Conservation Priority over Space and Time *
affiliations: and Universidad Privada Boliviana (UPB)

detail.title: The Readiness Option Conservation Priority over Space and Time *

declarations.funderStatement: Natural Environment Research Council (NERC)

detail.abstract:
Conservation allocation contains two related but distinct decisions: which places are valuable enough to secure, and when protection should occur. We develop a framework that separates siting priority-the contribution of a parcel to the conservation objective at a common date-from timing priority-the value of acting now rather than waiting for that parcel. Ecological quality and cross-site relevance determine why a parcel matters; evolving threat, acquisition cost, irreversibility, information, and institutional capacity determine when action is warranted. In a real-options model, early protection of high-value land can be optimal even when near-term conversion pressure is low. A favorable acquisition window may close before conversion is imminent, and protection can build readiness: legal precedent, administrative experience, public legitimacy, donor confidence, and political capacity that improve the feasibility or reduce the cost of later conservation action. 

The model yields a portfolio-conditioned structural-value screen, a distinct immediateaction cutoff, and an intermediate region in which a parcel has positive structural value but should not yet be protected. It also shows that, before the later intervention is imminent, the effect of uncertainty depends on initial institutional capacity. We then map these results to additionality. Finite-horizon avoided loss is an essential impact measure for some policy instruments, but an additionality eligibility or ranking constraint implements the conservation agency's choice only when it preserves both cross-site rankings and within-site timing. Readiness can also deter a contest before it forms, creating focal avoided loss that a contest-only measure misses. When development blocked at the focal parcel follows a less damaging continuation path, protection improves the wider landscape rather than merely relocating harm.

title: Efficient Capital, Inefficient Markets: Gender Bias, Structural Underfunding of Women-Led Startups and the Misallocation of Venture Capital

detail.abstract:
Female-founded companies generate 78 cents in revenue for every dollar raised, while their male-founded counterparts generate 31 cents. For decades, the companies producing more than twice the return per dollar of capital deployed have received less than two percent of available venture capital, underlining a massive allocation failure.

Venture capital markets are predicated on the assumption that capital flows toward the highest return. A persistent performance differential of this magnitude should, over time, produce a corresponding correction in where capital goes, but it has not. The thirty-year average allocation to all-female founding teams is 2.4 percent, holding across the internet expansion, post-2008 VC scaling, and multiple DEI commitment cycles.

This paper pursues what actually sustains this funding gap by drawing on frameworks from cognitive psychology and economics and cross-sector data from the United States, India, and Europe. It identifies the mechanisms through which evaluation distortion is reproduced at every stage of the investment cycle and the specific conditions under which the gap closes. At scale, the unrealised value creation from this misallocation runs to the trillions. The question remains whether the VCs deploying capital at below-optimal returns will recognise the financial incentive to demand fair allocation or not.

title: Return Asymmetry in the Market for Counter-Strike 2 In-Game Items

detail.abstract: This paper examines the market for Counter-Strike 2 in-game items over the period 2014–2026 and identifies a return asymmetry: items with certain characteristics consistently and substantially outperform items that lack them. Our regression analysis identifies starting price as the key return driver: items with a lower entry price exhibit significantly higher percentage returns (the low-base effect), whereas rarity tier and weapon type make no significant contribution to returns once starting price is controlled for. Descriptive analysis reveals that discontinued cases (those removed from the active drop pool) generate higher returns, although this effect is intertwined with case age. A comparison of case and content price dynamics shows that case returns consistently exceed the returns of their contents: in 80.95% of observations, the case proved to be the higher-return asset. The observed asymmetry is driven by the presence of a fixed-cost component in the case-opening cost structure (the key price), which amplifies the percentage price increase of the case when the value of its contents rises. This study demonstrates that the CS2 skins market is heterogeneous with respect to return drivers: identifiable parameters exist along which the investment attractiveness of assets can be differentiated. The practical implication is that the highest percentage returns in the CS2 skins market are consistently delivered by low-starting-price assets—cheap cases and skins in the lowest rarity tiers.

title: No Product No Brand: An Operational Definition of Luxury
affiliations: SDA Bocconi

detail.title: No Product No Brand: An Operational Definition of Luxury
detail.abstract: The literature on luxury branding employs between two and ten different dimensions to describe the same phenomenon, with little agreement on what is actually being measured. This article starts from the premise that this terminological proliferation stems from an error regarding the level of analysis: the brand rather than the product. Without an operational definition of the luxury product — its observable, and where possible measurable, material, productive, and economic properties — luxury-branding constructs remain floating signifiers, neither independently falsifiable nor measurable of the perceptions they claim to explain. Building on the product/brand/service distinction that recurs, unresolved, throughout the luxury-branding literature, this article proposes an operational definition of the luxury product along eight observable dimensions and a two-level framework in which luxury branding is redefined as a system of meaning constructed on top of — and not in place of — an operationally defined luxury product. An illustrative case comparing two structurally near-identical luxury watches that diverge widely in secondary-market value shows the two-level framework at work.

title: Photovoltaic Deployment Priorities Diverge from Plant-Scale Life-Cycle Mitigation Benefits in China
affiliations: Beijing Jiaotong University, Beijing Jiaotong University and Beijing Jiaotong University

detail.title: Photovoltaic Deployment Priorities Diverge from Plant-Scale Life-Cycle Mitigation Benefits in China
detail.abstract: Photovoltaic (PV) power is widely expected to advance Sustainable Development Goal (SDG) 7 and SDG 13 simultaneously, yet whether resource- and demand-oriented deployment translates into life-cycle mitigation benefits at the plant scale remains unclear. Here we develop an integrated framework combining supplier-specific module carbon footprints, actual plant-level electricity flows, provincial grid life-cycle carbon intensities and multi-indicator weighting. We analyse 10954 annual operating records from 3155 PV power plants in China during 2016–2023 and project the performance of 5016 planned plants through 2028. Operational losses increased the carbon intensity of exported electricity by 27.43% relative to theoretical generation in 2023. Deployment suitability and mitigation benefits were only weakly correlated, with 46.21% of existing plants showing conflicting classifications. In East China, 49.28% of plants had high deployment suitability but relatively low mitigation benefits, whereas in Northeast China, 67.80% had relatively low suitability but high mitigation benefits. The conflict share is projected to decline to 24.16% by 2028, with North China approaching alignment between deployment suitability and mitigation benefits. These results show that macro-level synergies between clean-energy expansion and climate action do not automatically translate into plant-level mitigation gains, and support incorporating life-cycle mitigation into PV siting and project prioritization.

title: Explainability-aware Supplier Reconfiguration under Disruption: A Synthetic Decision Experiment and Agent-based Benchmark for Egypt

detail.title: Explainability-aware Supplier Reconfiguration under Disruption: A Synthetic Decision Experiment and Agent-based Benchmark for Egypt
detail.abstract: This computational article evaluates an explainability-aware decision-support pipeline for selective supplier reconfiguration. Six hundred synthetic decision episodes crossed three explanation conditions with two disruptionseverity conditions. A simulated trust response incorporated explanation design, recommendation accuracy, severity, and random heterogeneity. The trust model explained 33.2% of variance. Synthetic trust was the dominant predictor of recommendation adoption in the logistic model (coefficient=0.68; AUC=0.68). Under severe disruption, operationalnarrative explanations produced a mean adoption rate of 76% and recovery time of 25.1 days, compared with 44% and 30.1 days without explanation. The study validates a computational analysis pipeline; it provides no evidence about actual managerial psychology or Egyptian decision makers.

title: The Information Isomorphism Law: A Meta-law Spanning Ontology and Epistemology --Tracing the Necessary Premise from the Cross-disciplinary Success of the Scientific Discovery Operating System

detail.title: The Information Isomorphism Law: A Meta-law Spanning Ontology and Epistemology --Tracing the Necessary Premise from the Cross-disciplinary Success of the Scientific Discovery Operating System
detail.abstract: The Scientific Discovery Operating System (Tang, 2026g, 2026r) has been successfully deployed across six completely independent disciplines, yet a fundamental question has never been systematically addressed: Why is this operating system effective? This paper's answer is: because in complex systems grounded in objective data and exhibiting regime switching, statistical structures carry the information of regime structures. This ontological fact is formally named herein as the Information Isomorphism Law. The argumentative path of this paper is not induction from specific discoveries to a universal principle, but a retracing from the operating system's success to its necessary premise: the six functional dimensions of the Testability Norms—Search Completeness, Modulation Relationship, Structural Breakpoints, Causal Direction, Problem Completeness, and Process Closure—together constitute a multi-dimensional probe of statistical structures. If statistical structures contained no information traces of regime switching, this methodology could not have succeeded repeatedly across six disciplines. Therefore, the success of the operating system itself proves the establishment of the Information Isomorphism Law. The Chow F-order parameter duality (Tang, 2026k) and the intercept/slope ratio-critical distance duality (Tang, 2026x, Theorem A) provide precision verification for this law on a truth-known system, rather than serving as its inductive basis. The Information Isomorphism Law is an ontological law—it asserts a fundamental fact about how the world is organized: "Statistical structures carry the information of regime structures." Precisely because it describes the special fact of "information carrying," it is naturally and simultaneously an epistemological meta-law—it answers the fundamental question of "how we can know the world." The Factor Hierarchy Law (likewise a meta-law) simultaneously revealed, at the moment of its discovery, both an organizational principle of the world and the statistical visibility of that principle—it inherently carries an epistemological dimension. The Information Isomorphism Law is the universalized extraction of this original unity—it separates "visibility" from the specific content of the Factor Hierarchy Law and establishes it as a universal law applicable to all regime switching across all statistical dimensions. The two laws are complementary, jointly constituting the complete philosophical foundation of the Scientific Discovery Operating System. Within the operating system, the Information Isomorphism Law occupies the epistemological foundation layer, completing a comprehensive four-layer structure. It must be candidly acknowledged that the Information Isomorphism Law was explicitly proposed only after the completion of the preceding 28 papers—historically, the operating system was successfully deployed first, and only later understood as to why it is effective. The contribution of this paper lies not in "inventing" information isomorphism, but in explicitly naming and systematically demonstrating this law for the first time, thereby completing the epistemological closure of the operating system.

title: Information Isomorphism Epistemology: From the Factor Hierarchy Law to the Reconstruction of Knowability -How the Establishment of an Original Epistemological Operating System Renders Kant's "Thing-in-Itself" Unnecessary

detail.title: Information Isomorphism Epistemology: From the Factor Hierarchy Law to the Reconstruction of Knowability -How the Establishment of an Original Epistemological Operating System Renders Kant's "Thing-in-Itself" Unnecessary
detail.abstract: This paper presents the establishment process of an original epistemological system—Information Isomorphism Epistemology—and its philosophical consequences for Kantian agnosticism. This system consists of four components, each with an independent origin and irreplaceable demonstrative function. The Law of Information Isomorphism reveals that in complex systems based on objective data and exhibiting regime switches, statistical structures carry information about regime structures—the Chow F achieves a globally unique maximum at the precise phase transition temperature, with deviation strictly zero in the analytic sense. The Factor Hierarchy Law reveals that any complex system is organized by a hierarchical structure of regime factors and execution factors—this is a cross-disciplinary, universal, formal meta-law of meta-laws that emerged from financial data and has been repeatedly verified across six completely independent disciplines. The Principle of Testability stipulates that any claim about factor importance in multi-factor systems must pass complete regime-dependence tests—claiming that "this factor is important" without specifying "under which regime" is an incomplete proposition. The Norms of Testability provide standardized testing procedures across six functional dimensions—functional dimensions remain relatively stable while implementation tools are replaceable. The four components, each independently originated, together constitute a complete epistemological system. The establishment of this system was not aimed at refuting agnosticism. Its starting point was a concrete methodological question. However, after its completion, a previously unforeseen philosophical consequence emerged: within the domain of scientific practice, the Law of Information Isomorphism replaces the function of the "thing-in-itself" as a specific explanatory item; the Principle of Testability blocks the retreat of "this is merely your subjective illusion"; the Norms of Testability provide a complete set of testing procedures and negative controls, making scientific practice equipped with this operating system no longer need to appeal to an unknowable "thing-in-itself" to guarantee its objectivity. The core argument of this paper can be summarized as "tool replacement"—not proving Kant wrong through philosophical debate, but using an original epistemological operating system to render the "thing-in-itself" no longer bearing any indispensable function in scientific practice.

title: Third-Person Epistemology: Information Isomorphism Epistemology and the Objective Foundation of Testability

detail.title: Third-Person Epistemology: Information Isomorphism Epistemology and the Objective Foundation of Testability
detail.abstract: This paper argues that Information Isomorphism Epistemology completes a paradigm shift in epistemology from the first person to the third person. Since Descartes, epistemology has been constructed in the first person—"I think," "I posit," "I see." When two "I"s reach conflicting conclusions, there is no public procedure to adjudicate. Information Isomorphism Epistemology is constructed in the third person: anyone, anywhere, downloading the publicly available data and running the same code, will obtain the same regime-switching structures. The argument proceeds from four mutually independent and mutually reinforcing pillars. First Pillar: The 2D Ising exact solution—the Chow F achieves a globally unique maximum at the precise phase transition temperature, with a deviation strictly zero in the analytic sense. Second Pillar: The 3D Ising double-peak fission—the algorithm, without any physical knowledge, proactively discovered a regime-switching structure previously unknown. Third Pillar: Cross-disciplinary emergence—the Factor Hierarchy Law has emerged repeatedly across six completely independent disciplines. Fourth Pillar: Tool replaceability—eight tools based on entirely different mathematical principles all converge near the confirmed breakpoints. These four pillars jointly point to a verified ontological fact: correct propositions leave detectable traces in statistical structures. From this fact, a criterion is derived: an epistemological system that makes factual claims about the empirical world must itself be testable. The legitimacy of this criterion does not derive from conceptual analysis but from the objective foundation jointly supported by these four pillars. Judged by this criterion, Descartes' "I think," Kant's "the thing-in-itself is unknowable," and Popper's falsifiability standard—all three have failed, in practice, to provide any public procedure satisfying the standard of traceability. Then, judged by the same criterion, Information Isomorphism Epistemology itself—each of its four components makes factual claims about the world, and each has passed the proposer's self-test. Information Isomorphism Epistemology is equally strict with itself, provides explicit falsification conditions, and bears the risk of being empirically overturned.

title: Cryptocurrency Adoption in Accounting: Challenges in Fair Value Measurement, Financial Reporting, and Accounting Information Systems
affiliations: University of Peshawar

detail.title: Cryptocurrency Adoption in Accounting: Challenges in Fair Value Measurement, Financial Reporting, and Accounting Information Systems
detail.abstract: The rapid growth of cryptocurrencies has created significant challenges for financial reporting systems that were not designed for decentralized and highly volatile digital assets. This study examines how publicly listed companies recognize, measure, and disclose cryptocurrencies in their financial statements under IFRS and U.S. GAAP, while also exploring the role of Accounting Information Systems (AIS) in supporting cryptocurrency accounting practices. Using a qualitative, interpretivist approach, the study conducts content analysis of audited annual financial statements from six cryptocurrency-exposed companies: Tesla, MicroStrategy, CleanSpark, Riot Platforms, Galaxy Digital, and PayPal. The analysis focuses on accounting policies, asset classification, measurement methods, impairment treatment, disclosure practices, risk reporting, and AIS capabilities. The findings reveal a strong tendency to classify cryptocurrencies as intangible assets, while excluding them from cash and financial instrument categories. However, differences remain in measurement and disclosure practices. Overall, the study contributes to the growing literature on cryptocurrency accounting by providing evidence from actual corporate reporting practices and highlighting ongoing challenges related to comparability, transparency, and system readiness.

title: The Role of Turkiye’s Syrian Policy in Redefining its Relations with NATO in 2011–2024

detail.title: The Role of Turkiye’s Syrian Policy in Redefining its Relations with NATO in 2011–2024
detail.abstract: The major research problem of this thesis is Turkish policy towards Syria and its impact on Turkiye’s relations with NATO. It is important for the studies on Turkish foreign policy and NATO, and fills the gap in the literature. It focuses on the Syrian civil war, Turkiye’s military operations, and the nationalist group's collaboration with the Turkish government, showing how it redefined Turkiye-NATO relations. The descriptive chapter examines how the strategic depth policy shaped Turkish-Syrian policy and the role of Turkiye’s negotiations on Syria. The analytical chapter explores how the Kurdish movement in Syria and Turkiye’s military operations affected Turkiye’s relations with NATO. The thesis seeks to evaluate Turkiye’s role in NATO over the 13 years of its Syrian policy.

title:
From Buy-and-Hold to Buy-and-Help: 

A Value-Creation Capability for Asset Owners
affiliations: Stanford University, University of California Office of Chief Investment Officer,  and

detail.title:
From Buy-and-Hold to Buy-and-Help: 

A Value-Creation Capability for Asset Owners

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Ashby Monk and Jagdeep Bachher co-developed the value-creation approach still in use at UC Investments. Ashby Monk and Evan Greenfield have collaborated on value-creation projects with asset owners. Ashby Monk and Pandu Sjahrir are developing a new value-creation team drawing on the findings in this paper. Ashby Monk is developing a commercial technology informed by aspects of this research.
declarations.funderStatement: The authors thank the institutions that opened their organizations to this research and the colleagues and affiliates of Stanford Long-Term Investing (SLTI) who contributed to this research agenda. Any remaining errors or omissions are our own.

detail.abstract: Long-term asset owners have spent decades professionalizing how capital is allocated and invested, but far less attention has been devoted to how post-investment experience is recognized, transferred, and reused. This learning gap is particularly consequential for large asset owners. Their breadth, duration, and relational span expose them repeatedly to related problems across companies, managers, asset classes, geographies, and market cycles, while knowledge and decision rights remain distributed among actors they do not control. We call this structural condition 'asset-owner positionality': a potential learning advantage rooted in 'brokerage without command.' Drawing on more than a decade of fieldwork and capability-design engagements, public examples from leading asset owners, and research on organizational learning and knowledge transfer, we identify recurring breakdowns that prevent this positionality advantage from being realized and propose a thin horizontal Value-Creation Capability ("VCC") as the conversion mechanism. The VCC identifies financially material recurring problems, maps prior cases and relevant expertise, brings that experience into later comparable decisions, and captures what is learned for reuse. In economic terms, it seeks economies of scope in post-investment learning. We envision 'buy-and-help' as an evolution of buy-and-hold: not greater or more centralized control, but more capable ownership that systematically converts repeated experience into compounding institutional capability.

title: The Measurement of U.S. Tariffs in 2025
affiliations: United States International Trade Commission (USITC) and

detail.title: The Measurement of U.S. Tariffs in 2025

publicationDetails.detailsText: USITC Office of Economics Working Paper 2026-07-D

detail.abstract: This paper documents and compares data sources and methods that measure U.S. tariff rates in 2025. We outline key points related to accurately tracking tariff changes, such as establishing a baseline, accounting for exemptions and stacking rules, distinguishing statutory from applied rates, and managing product-level concordances and aggregation choices. The paper plots the evolution of average U.S. tariff rates using five tariff measures. Two tariff measures are constructed with publicly available data on calculated duties and customs values from official U.S. government trade data, and three tariff measures are from publicly available datasets in the academic literature that track tariff changes over the year. These measures generally document increases in tariff rates over March and April 2025, with variation in the magnitude of tariff rates depending on the tariff data source. We also document substantial variation in U.S. tariff rates across trading partners and industries. Finally, alternative aggregation approaches of U.S. tariff rates are shown to have meaningful impacts on the average U.S. tariff rate.

title: From Tariff to Award II: Determinants of Court-Awarded Litigation Costs in Civil Appeals before Swiss Cantonal High Courts

detail.title: From Tariff to Award II: Determinants of Court-Awarded Litigation Costs in Civil Appeals before Swiss Cantonal High Courts
detail.abstract:
Swiss cantons set the tariffs for litigation costs, but courts retain discretion within them. This study examines how court-awarded litigation costs at cantonal high courts relate to the applicable tariff, case characteristics, and procedural features, and how well such awards can be predicted at the time an appeal is filed. The source corpus contains 8,120 published civil-chamber judgments from the high courts of Aargau, Grisons, Solothurn, Zug, and Zurich for the period from 1 January 2011 to 31 December 2025. The analysis sample comprises 3,368 pecuniary appeals (Berufung, Art. 308 et seq. CPC) with a stated appeal value of at least CHF 10,000, coded across 58 variables. Tariff regressions are limited to Zurich, Aargau, and Zug, where the tariff baseline can be reconstructed mechanically.

For positive court-cost awards, the deviation model indicates compression: awards rise less than proportionally with the tariff baseline, with a headline elasticity of about 0.69. The result is strongest in Zurich, which accounts for 92 percent of the court-cost regression sample, and is weaker and estimator-dependent in Aargau and Zug. Two further associations recur in all five published court samples. A positive party-compensation award is observed in 80 percent of appeals with an appeal response and in 8 percent without one. The first-instance cost award is modified in 64 percent of appeals in which the appellant carries no loss share and in 5 percent in which the appellant carries the full loss share. At the filing stage, the tariff baseline and the observed case profile yield a useful central estimate of a positive award, but the in-sample 90 percent residual limits run from roughly 0.3 to 3.4 times the point forecast. The design is explanatory and ex post, and the estimates are associations rather than causal effects. Results are conditional on the published subset of judgments.

This is Part II of a three-part series.

title: The Two Faces of Risk in the Tragedy of the Commons: Risk Aversion, Price Uncertainty, and Strategic Resource Exploitation
affiliations: University of Glasgow, Umeå University and

detail.title: The Two Faces of Risk in the Tragedy of the Commons: Risk Aversion, Price Uncertainty, and Strategic Resource Exploitation
detail.abstract: We study how risk aversion and uncertainty shape the strategic exploitation of a common-property resource. We develop a continuous-time stochastic differential game in which heterogeneous agents extract a renewable resource non-cooperatively while facing two correlated sources of uncertainty, shocks to the resource stock and fluctuations in the output price. We implement the model in a fishery setting, with logistic biomass growth, stochastic recruitment, and a geometric Brownian output price, providing a concrete environment for mechanisms that extend more broadly to competitively exploited renewable resources. The resulting coupled Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equations are solved numerically using finite differences and policy iteration, with the solution method validated against an analytically tractable linear-quadratic benchmark. Our results reveal two opposing faces of risk in the tragedy of the commons. Greater risk aversion reduces equilibrium extraction and thereby mitigates over-exploitation, acting as a partial substitute for cooperation. Although it does not eliminate the strategic externality, risk aversion reduces aggregate extraction by up to roughly forty percent in our experiments, while welfare measured in a common monetary metric increases. By contrast, greater price uncertainty increases extraction once agents are risk-averse, as agents accelerate the conversion of uncertain future resource revenues into current returns. This volatility channel is essentially absent under risk neutrality. These opposing effects distinguish greater aversion to risk from greater exposure to risk and help reconcile conflicting findings in the literature on uncertainty and commonproperty resource exploitation. We further show how the two channels interact with heterogeneity in extraction costs, with implications for the management of strategically exploited renewable resources.

title:
Beyond Raw Mineral Exports 

Generative Economic Intelligence for Critical-Mineral Industrialization in Africa
affiliations: Independent

detail.title:
Beyond Raw Mineral Exports 

Generative Economic Intelligence for Critical-Mineral Industrialization in Africa
detail.abstract: Africa's strategic importance in global critical-mineral supply chains has intensified alongside rising demand for minerals required for electrification, clean-energy technologies, digital infrastructure, and advanced manufacturing. Yet mineral abundance does not automatically translate into domestic industrial value creation. This paper introduces Generative Economic Intelligence (GEN-EI) as an evidence-grounded framework for transforming heterogeneous economic data, empirical analysis, scenario simulations, and robustness testing into decisionoriented economic intelligence. The framework is applied to four country-mineral cases: Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) cobalt, DRC copper, Zambia copper, and Guinea's bauxite-alumina-aluminium value chain. Bilateral trade data are used to classify exports across raw, intermediate, refined, and downstream processing stages and to construct measures of processing depth. Poisson Pseudo-Maximum Likelihood (PPML) models examine conditional relationships between processing stage and bilateral export performance, while hydropower indicators provide a diagnostic dimension of the enabling environment for deeper processing. Scenario analysis estimates potential additional domestic value capture under alternative transformation assumptions, followed by sensitivity testing across 25 parameter combinations. The results reveal sharply differentiated industrial positions. Guinea remains concentrated in raw bauxite exports and exhibits the largest relative scenario opportunity; DRC copper combines an established refining position with substantial additional value-capture potential; Zambia exhibits significant intermediate and refined copper capabilities; and DRC cobalt is already concentrated around refined and chemical processing. Across all 25 sensitivity combinations, the relative GDP-equivalent opportunity ranking remains unchanged: Guinea bauxite, DRC copper, Zambia copper, and DRC cobalt. These results are conditional scenario magnitudes rather than forecasts of GDP growth. The paper demonstrates that African critical-mineral strategies should not be reduced to a uniform prescription to 'process more locally.' GEN-EI instead asks which next stage of transformation is economically credible for each country-mineral system given its existing position, potential value capture, enabling conditions, and implementation constraints.

title: A Static Model for Quantifying the Fiscal Effects of Humanoid Robot Adoption
affiliations: Universidad Complutense de Madrid (UCM)

detail.title: A Static Model for Quantifying the Fiscal Effects of Humanoid Robot Adoption
detail.abstract: This paper develops a comparative-static analytical framework to evaluate the fiscal implications of largescale humanoid robot adoption. The model integrates the principal channels through which labour displacement affects public finances, including social security contributions, personal income taxation, value-added tax revenues, and expenditure on a guaranteed minimum-income programme. These fiscal effects are balanced against new revenue sources arising from robot taxation, corporate income taxation associated with domestic value creation, and import duties. The framework derives the conditions under which robot adoption remains fiscally neutral and demonstrates that fiscal sustainability depends on the joint interaction of labour-market adjustment, redistribution policies, industrial structure, and trade policy. Rather than identifying a unique robot tax, the model characterises a fiscal neutrality frontier (FNF) consisting of all policy combinations that preserve fiscal balance. The analysis therefore shifts the debate from the taxation of robots alone to the design of a coherent fiscal architecture capable of sustaining public finances in increasingly automated economies.

detail.abstract: Existing literature discusses e-Governance, Digital Public Infrastructure, and AI governance largely as separate subjects addressed by distinct technical and policy communities. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, comparatively little published work explains their evolution through a single institutional-governance lens. This paper addresses that gap by tracing the institutional evolution of public governance in India across successive eras — the Administrative Era (1947–1980s), Early Computerisation (1990s–2005), e-Governance (2006–2014), Digital Public Infrastructure (2015–2022), and the emerging AI-assisted governance era (2023 onward). Using a conceptual, comparative-institutional method combining documentary analysis, historical periodisation, and diagrammatic synthesis, the paper distinguishes institution, government and governance as analytically separate concepts and shows how the chain of legal authority running from the Constitution to the individual citizen-facing decision has persisted even as the unit of administrative work has changed — from the physical file to the departmental database record to distributed, reusable digital-public-infrastructure data and now to AI-assisted decision support. The central finding is that while the instruments of governance have repeatedly changed — the constitutional obligation owed to the citizen — that a decision be lawful, fair, and explainable — has not. The paper further identifies six governance questions that AI-assisted administration newly poses to Indian public institutions: transparency, accountability, data quality, inclusion, human oversight, and record-keeping or data retention for audit purposes. It closes by arguing that the enduring task of the public officer across every era examined is to keep the chain of responsibility legible, whatever the technology of the day and by setting out directions for future empirical research.

title: Institutional Reform Without Democratization: Measuring the Gap Between Governance Change and Civic Freedom in Central Asia, 2016-2024

detail.abstract: Since 2016, Uzbekistan and Kazakhstan have launched sweeping "reform" agendas under the leadership of Shavkat Mirziyoyev and Kassym-Jomart Tokayev, respectively. Both presidents have publicly committed to modernizing state institutions, improving public services, and engaging with the international community after decades of sclerotic authoritarianism. However, a central question remains unanswered: Have these institutional reforms translated into meaningful gains in civic freedom and political rights, or are they primarily cosmetic adjustments designed to stabilize hybrid authoritarian rule? This paper employs a mixed-methods approach, combining quantitative analysis of V-Dem, Freedom House, and World Bank Worldwide Governance Indicators (WGI) from 2016 to 2024 with a qualitative case study of Uzbekistan. The study compares Uzbekistan, Kazakhstan, and the more politically open Kyrgyzstan. Findings reveal a persistent and widening governance-freedom gap: while indices measuring state capacity and regulatory quality have modestly improved, indicators of liberal democracy, freedom of expression, and civil liberties remain at extreme authoritarian levels. The paper argues that these reforms constitute a sophisticated form of authoritarian upgrading-enhancing the performance of the state without ceding political power-and discusses the implications for international engagement with Central Asia.

detail.abstract: This research develops an integrated, testable framework for helping income-poor and vulnerable families progress from consumption insecurity to durable economic selfsufficiency. It synthesizes global evidence on social protection, Graduation-style economic inclusion, human capital, financial inclusion, enterprise development, labor-market activation, gender, health, and climate resilience, and interprets lessons from Cambodia and five ASEAN role models: Viet Nam, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia, and the Philippines. The central finding is that no single instrument reliably solves persistent poverty. Transfers protect minimum consumption; productive grants or assets relax capital constraints; coaching, skills, savings, market access, care services, health coverage, and shock-responsive protection address complementary barriers. Credit can support already viable cash flows but is unsafe as the default entry instrument for debt-stressed households. The proposed Household Economic Self-Sufficiency Framework uses five stages-stabilize, diagnose, build capabilities, invest and connect, and protect and graduate-supported by household case management, transparent targeting, local market diagnostics, digital monitoring, grievance redress, and independent evaluation. A Cambodia pilot design, governance model, board scorecard, and 36-month roadmap are provided. Because this is a framework paper rather than a completed impact evaluation, numerical targets are explicitly identified as proposed benchmarks and must not be read as causal findings. The paper concludes that policy should optimize resilient net household income and agency, not program exit alone.

title: Professional Identity and Economic Decision-Making among Chinese Future Physicians

detail.abstract: We use a professional-identity priming experiment to study the behavioral content of the norms that Chinese medical students associate with being a physician, and how that content evolves over medical education. In the experiment, 198 medical students in western China are randomly assigned to answer questions that make their identity as a future physician salient, or neutral filler questions, before completing six incentivized tasks. For first-year students, the physician-identity prime has no effect that survives inference. The robust finding is a difference by stage of training: relative to first-year students, priming makes fourth-year students significantly less altruistic in monetary allocations but more willing to acquire payoff-relevant information, even when that information constrains self-interested action. These two effects work in opposite directions and roughly offset each other. Such a heterogeneous priming effect is consistent with professional socialization reshaping the behavioral content of the physician identity over the course of professional training.

title: The Scope of Universality: Identity Essentialism and the Limits of Moral Universalism
affiliations: Radboud University

detail.title: The Scope of Universality: Identity Essentialism and the Limits of Moral Universalism
detail.abstract: While universalism is foundational to inclusive cooperation, existing research has difficulty separating two dimensions of moral boundaries: the scope of people’s universality and the intensity of their ethical concern for all others. This paper introduces identity essentialism, the belief that group identities and boundaries are immutable and impermeable, as the key psychological factor shaping how inclusively societies or individuals define the scope of their universality, independent of the associated intensity of concern. I employ a radius decomposition of expressions of concern for “humankind” to assess the degree to which societal and individual construals of this abstract concern are localized, in-group-connoted versus genuinely universalist, out-group-connoted. Utilizing a deep-rooted linguistic trait as an instrument, I demonstrate that identity essentialism causally contracts the radius of moral universality. This quantified moral universality radius is wholly independent from group-specific moral concerns and outperforms kinship intensity in predicting macro-level prosociality and impartial institutions. My findings indicate that formally universalist sentiment frequently reflects parochial moral concern extended nominally to humankind rather than genuine out-group concern. This uncovers a structural limit to moral universalism that we would miss if we focused solely on differences in the intensity of moral preferences across pre-defined groups.

title: When Does Exponential Utility Give Reliable Portfolio Advice?

detail.title: When Does Exponential Utility Give Reliable Portfolio Advice?
detail.abstract: Exponential utility is often used as a tractable surrogate for wealth-dependent risk preferences. We ask whether matching absolute risk aversion at current wealth preserves even the direction of an optimal portfolio recommendation. Holding the centered distribution of risk fixed, we vary only its compensation, measured by the Sharpe ratio. At low Sharpe ratios, matched CARA over-invests in negatively skewed risks and under-invests in positively skewed ones. At high Sharpe ratios, however, the comparison changes. If the worst outcome is an isolated atom, strict decreasing absolute risk aversion implies eventual CARA under-investment, irrespective of skewness, conditional on an interior optimum. With a continuous lower endpoint, this conclusion fails: the sign depends on how probability mass behaves near the worst outcome, and DARA alone no longer determines it. For CRRA, a sharp ordering and explicit limiting position ratios are recovered. Thus exact local calibration need not remain directionally reliable as the same underlying risk becomes better compensated.

title: Immigration Enforcement and Local Business Dynamics
affiliations: and University of Alabama at Birmingham

detail.title: Immigration Enforcement and Local Business Dynamics
detail.abstract: This paper examines the effects of interior immigration enforcement on local business dynamics. Exploiting the federally determined rollout of the Secure Communities program across U.S. counties, we use county-sector-year Census administrative data to show that enforcement reduces firm and establishment counts by suppressing establishment entry, with no significant effect on establishment exit. These effects are concentrated in high-immigrant counties and in immigrant-intensive, high-turnover, and non-tradable sectors, suggesting that immigration enforcement constrains business growth through reduced labor availability and local demand. Enforcement also reduces job creation, with the decline driven primarily by continuing establishments reducing expansion.

title: Risk Spillover Effects Among Chinese Financial Institutions: Evidence from a Complex-Network Perspective
affiliations: Jinan University - Finance Department

detail.title: Risk Spillover Effects Among Chinese Financial Institutions: Evidence from a Complex-Network Perspective
detail.abstract: This paper studies the systemic risk spillover dynamics of 34 Chinese financial institutions over the 2014-2023 rolling-window evaluation period. Using weekly data, a single-index-model (SIM) quantile regression framework, and rolling-window estimation, the paper estimates institution-level Value-at-Risk (VaR) and Conditional Value-at-Risk (CoVaR), measures the overall systemic risk level of China's financial system, and constructs a tail-event-driven network of risk spillovers. The empirical analysis further traces the dynamic evolution of spillover topology, identifies the main spillover senders and receivers, and evaluates systemically important financial institutions by combining connectedness measures with market capitalization. Four results stand out. First, extreme shocks make systemic linkages significantly tighter and raise total network connectedness. Second, most systemic risk transmission occurs within the same sector, while cross-sector spillovers are comparatively limited. Third, banks and securities firms are the dominant sources and recipients of systemic spillovers during most of the sample period, whereas insurance firms remain less interconnected. Fourth, banks generally exhibit higher systemic importance than securities firms and insurers, and several large banks emerge as China's systemically important financial institutions.

title: Annealed Random Operators for Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Annealed Random Operators for Reinforcement Learning
detail.abstract: Polson and Sorensen (2011) solve the Bellman equation by iterating a random Monte Carlo operator built from a simulated-annealing kernel. We show that the annealed backup they use, the expectation of Q under a Boltzmann kernel, is neither monotone nor a sup-norm non-expansion, and exhibit a two-state Markov decision process whose annealed Bellman equation has three solutions, the symmetric one having Jacobian spectral radius 1.176; value iteration converges to a spurious branch selected by the starting point. The condition λ > λ ⋆ is therefore substantive, and λ ⋆ depends on unobservable Q-value gaps. Replacing the Boltzmann average by the mellowmax certainty equivalent, whose gradient is exactly the kernel the algorithm already samples from, gives an unconditional β-contraction. This removes λ > λ ⋆ , the compactness and unique-argmax hypotheses and the quadratic remainder, sharpens the geometric factor from (1 + β)/2 to β, and costs an explicit O(λ-1) bias. A Bernstein bound in place of Chebyshev cuts the Monte Carlo budget by 4.0 × 10 4 at our scale, and an annealed (λ g , M g) schedule restores geometric convergence to Q ⋆. Empirically the rate is β to four digits; on pendulum swing-up we match tabular Q-learning's accuracy at 4 × 10 7 transitions using 1.9 × 10 6 ; relative accuracy holds near 1% from d = 1 to d = 12; and Anderson acceleration, which the annealed operator's smoothness makes well conditioned, cuts the rate to 0.135. Finally we correct a conflation in the risk-sensitive extension the original paper proposed: the entropic transform acts on the state integral, not the decision reduction. Risk sensitivity moves portfolios into the interior but does not cure the ill-conditioning behind extremal allocations.

title: Multi-Credit Calibration via Elastically Stopped Lévy Processes
affiliations: Columbia University and

detail.title: Multi-Credit Calibration via Elastically Stopped Lévy Processes
detail.abstract: We calibrate credit default swaps and index tranches with elastically stopped Lévy processes: each firm defaults when the running supremum of a latent, spectrally positive distress process crosses an independent exponential barrier. This yields a Cox construction with totally inaccessible default times, while retaining the interpretability and explicit formulas of a structural approach. Adding a single common compound Poisson jump factor to every firm's latent driver gives a parsimonious multi-credit model with simultaneous defaults, which is priced by an exact Wiener-Hopf Monte Carlo scheme. Its tractability rests on a single-name result we prove: a finite partial-fraction formula for the Laplace transform of the default probability under phase-type jumps. On daily CDX North American High-Yield and Investment-Grade panels, our drivers attain the lowest out-of-sample errors in a six-model field and reproduce the inverted spread curves of names heading into default, which a Lévy subordinator provably does not. At the index level, the two-parameter dependence structure closes 73% to 89% of the tranche pricing gap left by independent marginals with the dependence parameters frozen, and up to 95% once remarked to tranche quotes; our framework dominates a single-factor Gaussian copula and the affine intensity benchmark of Duffie-Gârleanu on both indices.

title: Beyond Account Growth: Assessing the Contribution of Mobile Financial Services to Financial Inclusion in Bangladesh
affiliations: National University of Bangladesh, , National University, Bangladesh, National University of Bangladesh and National University of Bangladesh

detail.title: Beyond Account Growth: Assessing the Contribution of Mobile Financial Services to Financial Inclusion in Bangladesh
detail.abstract: Mobile Financial Services (MFS) have become a cornerstone of Bangladesh's digital economy since their launch in 2011, offering a low-cost channel through which a historically unbanked population can access formal financial services. This study quantitatively examines the growth trajectory of MFS adoption in Bangladesh and its association with financial inclusion, drawing on secondary time-series data published by Bangladesh Bank, the World Bank's Global Findex Database, and a range of academic and industry sources. MFS adoption is assessed through registered accounts, transaction value, and active agents, while financial inclusion is assessed through financial account ownership, mobile-money participation, and the gender gap in account ownership. The central finding is that although MFS expansion has substantially widened financial access in Bangladesh, growth in registered MFS accounts and transaction activity does not correspond one-for-one with growth in the number of newly, and genuinely, financially included individuals: the pace of improvement in overall account ownership slowed markedly after 2017 even as MFS accounts and transaction volumes continued to expand rapidly. The market, moreover, remains highly concentrated among a small number of providers. The study relies on descriptive and trend-based secondary-data methods rather than regression or structural modeling, and its findings are therefore interpreted as quantitative associations rather than estimates of causal effect. The study concludes that deepening genuine financial inclusion in Bangladesh will require a shift in policy emphasis from account proliferation toward active usage, savings, credit access, and financial resilience, and it proposes a primary-data research agenda for future causal testing of the adoptioninclusion relationship.

title: Constitutional Communications Governance in NewVistas through a Multiplex Network Framework for Interoperability Resilience and Access
affiliations: Quaid-i-Azam University and NewVistas Foundation

detail.title: Constitutional Communications Governance in NewVistas through a Multiplex Network Framework for Interoperability Resilience and Access
detail.abstract: Unlike conventional communications regulations, Agency 10 is not designed as a telecommunications operator, media authority, platform owner, content regulator, pricing body, underwriter, or surveillance institution. Its function is to govern the technical communications layer through device standards, interoperability requirements, emergencyalert capability, secure interfaces, accessibility rules, vendor-neutral compatibility, and communication-system exposure limits in shared environments. The paper proposes a multiplex communication-network resilience and interoperability framework to formalize this role. The framework models communications as a multilayer network linking residents, stewards, contractors, emergency nodes, governance offices, utilities, transport systems, devices, terminals, alerts, and service interfaces across five layers: device compatibility, interoperability/API integration, emergency signalling, accessibility, and shared-space exposure. Methodologically, it combines interoperability matrices, DeGroot signal-diffusion logic, spectral graph resilience, accessibility inclusion matrices, vendor-lock-in diagnostics, exposure constraints, and failure simulations. DeGroot modelling is used only to test emergency and operational signal reach, not ideological convergence or opinion formation. Spectral connectivity and centrality measures identify fragmentation risk, bottleneck dependence, and hidden vendor monopoly. Accessibility matrices test whether vulnerable and critical user groups retain redundant communication channels. Exposure constraints limit involuntary technological burden without regulating message content. The article’s main contribution is to show how communications standards can be made mathematically testable while remaining constitutionally bound. Agency 10 strengthens interoperability, emergency readiness, privacy, resilience, accessibility, and vendor neutrality without absorbing Agency 11 Proof, Agency 12 Media, Agency 14 Legal, Agency 17 Publication, Agency 20 Markets, Agency 21 Underwriting, Agency 23 Utilities, or Agency 24 Transportation. The framework contributes to network governance, institutional economics, digital constitutionalism, infrastructure resilience, accessibility governance, and AI-risk governance by demonstrating how robust communications infrastructure can be governed without becoming a monopoly, surveillance rail, content-control system, or platform state.

title: The Tiered Approval Bottleneck: A Case Study of Official Travel Payment (Perjadin) Disbursement in a Regional Government Audit Institution
affiliations: and

detail.title: The Tiered Approval Bottleneck: A Case Study of Official Travel Payment (Perjadin) Disbursement in a Regional Government Audit Institution
detail.abstract: Public financial management reform in Indonesia has increasingly emphasized digitalization as a lever for improving disbursement efficiency without weakening internal control. Yet much of the empirical literature on public-sector fiscal governance operates at the cross-jurisdictional or macro level, leaving the micro-level, single-unit operational dynamics of routine government payment workflows comparatively underexamined. This paper presents a qualitative single-case study of the official travel payment (Perjadin) disbursement workflow at the West Nusa Tenggara Provincial Representative Office of Indonesia's Financial and Development Supervisory Agency (BPKP), itself the country's apex internal government auditor. Data were collected through six weeks of structured participant observation and document review during a supervised internship placement within the office's Finance Sub-Coordinator unit. The workflow was mapped as a sixstage, six-party tiered authorization process and evaluated using SWOT analysis with IFAS/EFAS weighting. The case reveals a structurally sound control architecture, strong tiered authorization and pre-payment verification that nonetheless generates a persistent efficiency cost: disbursement delay driven by manual document routing and dependence on the physical availability of signing officials. The resulting strategic position (Quadrant I, aggressive strategy) suggests that targeted digitalization of the approval chain, rather than restructuring of the control architecture itself, is the most defensible reform path. The paper contributes an operational-level complement to existing fiscal-governance scholarship on digital transformation and control efficacy in Indonesian public financial management, and offers transferable, practitioner-oriented recommendations for comparable government units facing similar authorization-chain constraints.

title: The Nash Equilibrium Puzzle in Public Administration: From Suboptimal Outcomes to Systemic Equilibrium Traps

detail.title: The Nash Equilibrium Puzzle in Public Administration: From Suboptimal Outcomes to Systemic Equilibrium Traps
detail.abstract: Nash Equilibrium introduces a persistent theoretical anomaly within public administration research. Although scholars frequently deploy it as an analytical instrument to clarify entrenched, suboptimal administrative outcomes, applying these models prescriptively during policy formulation frequently yields limited success. The present investigation examines the mechanics underlying this discrepancy. Drawing upon a systematic synthesis of existing literature, the analysis suggests that such a disconnect likely originates from the highly restrictive premises of classical game theory, which generally omit the behavioral and evolutionary variables inherent in public sector operations. In an effort to address these theoretical limitations, a consolidated conceptual model termed "Systemic Equilibrium Traps" is proposed. Within this context, a trap is operationalized as a self-perpetuating, deficient condition maintained by the convergence of three intersecting strata. These include the formal Institutional Game regulating structural incentives, the Cognitive-Social Filter encompassing the heuristic norms guiding actor interpretation, and the Evolutionary Path dictating systemic resilience through learned dependencies. This multidimensional approach appears to provide a more nuanced mechanism for diagnosing persistent policy failures, thereby establishing a foundation for multi-tiered interventions directed at systemic dynamics and cognitive frameworks alongside traditional regulatory incentives.

title: Patriarchy Without Body: AI, Autonomous Weapons, and the Algorithmic Institutionalization of Militarized Masculinity

detail.title: Patriarchy Without Body: AI, Autonomous Weapons, and the Algorithmic Institutionalization of Militarized Masculinity
detail.abstract: The integration of artificial intelligence (AI), unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs), and autonomous weapons systems (AWS) into contemporary combat marks a structural transformation in how state violence 1 is organized and legitimized. This paper interrogates the extent to which AI-enabled warfare reconfigures the gendered logics of militarized masculinities, arguing that these technologies displace and rematerialize stereotypical gendered architecture. Drawing on feminist security studies, masculinities scholarship, and intersectional feminist theory, this analysis examines how militarized ideals of precision, emotional detachment, and technostrategic control, are increasingly encoded within algorithmic systems and autonomous platforms and systems. As the embodied soldier is progressively supplanted by remotely piloted and AI-driven systems, the physical markers that once anchored gendered identity in warfare, in that of proximity, bodily risk, and direct command are abstracted into decision-support software architectures. Through a comparative analysis of the Russian, Ukrainian, and Israeli Defense Forces operations, this paper demonstrates how these shifts manifest across drone command, agency, and conflict. It further contends that this abstraction renders the gendered distribution of power and violence less physical, complicating both scholarly critique and regulatory intervention. The paper concludes with policy recommendations toward autonomous weapons governance, contributing to emerging scholarship at the intersection of feminist security studies, military technology, and global security.

title: Institutional Quality, State Capacity, and Sustainable Development: A Global Analysis of SDG 16 Implementation
affiliations: and

detail.title: Institutional Quality, State Capacity, and Sustainable Development: A Global Analysis of SDG 16 Implementation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study is a review of published literature and did not involve human participants, animal subjects, or primary data collection; ethical approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: Sustainable Development Goal 16 was designed as the enabling goal of the 2030 Agenda, yet its own indicators are moving backwards: press freedom and perceived control of corruption have declined since 2015, and conflict deaths and forced displacement have reached their highest levels of the SDG era. This article reviews the cross-national evidence on SDG 16 implementation and asks why a goal so widely described as the foundation of the wider agenda behaves, in quantitative interaction studies, as one of its main obstacles. The review joins two research traditions that have developed largely in isolation. The institutional quality tradition treats institutions as constraints on power and links the rule of law, accountability, and corruption control to long-run development. The state capacity tradition treats institutions as instruments of power and asks whether states can tax, administer, and deliver. SDG 16 bundles both into a single goal, and the evidence indicates that the two dimensions neither move together across countries nor respond to the same reforms. The article develops a quality-capacity framework that sorts national implementation experiences into four profiles and derives four propositions about sequencing, measurement, and durability of progress. The framework resolves the enablerhurdle contradiction: SDG 16 enables the agenda where quality and capacity reinforce each other and obstructs it where they diverge. Implications for indicator design, Voluntary National Reviews, and the institutional role of higher education are drawn.

title: Female Labour Force Participation Rate (FLFPR) and State-Level Economic Performance in India: Evidence from Selected States
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Female Labour Force Participation Rate (FLFPR) and State-Level Economic Performance in India: Evidence from Selected States
detail.abstract: This study examines the relation between FLFPR and per capita Net State Domestic Product (NSDP) across eight major Indian states: Bihar, Gujarat, Karnataka, Kerala, Maharashtra, Tamil Nadu, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal, over the period 2012-2022. Using panel data with 48 observations, the paper employs pooled OLS, Fixed effects and Random Effects regression models and literacy rates as a human capital control variable. The Fixed Effect model finds that one percentage increase in FLFPR associates with 0.74% increase in the Log NSDP (p=0.033) after controlling for literacy and unobserved heterogeneity. The correlation between FLFPR and Log NSDP is observed to be strong (r=0.805) with literacy rates emerging as independently significant determinant of economic output. Regional sub-group analysis suggests that the FLFPR and growth relationships is most evident in the Southern states and was weaker in the western states with industrialization which reflects the institutional and structural heterogeneity across the states. Though the relationship was bidirectional and long-run rather than short-run in the lagged FLFPR model, it resulted in insignificance of the coefficient. FLFP can hence be established as a macroeconomic variable rather than a mere social equity indicator to close the female participation, one of the most underutilized growth levers in conjunction with literacy and educational investment.

detail.abstract: The study is conducted in order to measure the efficiency of 22 OECD countries by taking data of seven years from 2008-2014. The analysis is conducted by taking three input variables education spending, health spending and social spending. All three input variables are taken as percentage of GDP. Output variables include life expectancy at birth, Infant Survival Rate (ISR), 25-34 years old population with tertiary education, unemployment rate and Corruption index. DEA is employed to measure the technical efficiency of the selected DMUs under the assumptions of CRS and VRS and then Scale efficiency is calculated. There are 9 countries on the frontier under CRS while France is the least efficient one. Total efficiency under CRS is 94%. Under VRS 15 countries are on the frontier and the least efficient one is Belgium. Total efficiency under VRS is 97%. Switzerland is the least efficient country under Scale efficiency and there are 9 countries on the frontier. Total Scale Efficiency is 97%. Then second stage analysis is conducted in order to separately analyze the European and Non-European countries by taking VRS efficiency scores as dependent variable and the independent variables include GDP per capita growth rate, Government Stability, Income Inequality, Labor Force Participation rate (between 15-64 years), Human development Index (HDI) and one Dummy variable that take 1 for Non-European and 0 for European countries. The second stage analysis shows a significant positively related impact of GDP Per Capita Growth Rate and Government Stability over efficiency. Income inequality is negatively related and statistically significant while HDI is insignificant statistically as it is a combination variable. All the results for truncated regression are calculated at 95% confidence interval.

title: Formation and Fragility

detail.title: Formation and Fragility
detail.abstract: Vendor finance can both relax customer financing constraints and create the links along which distress later propagates. Existing trade-credit theory explains why bilateral contracts form, while financial-network theory studies amplification on a given network. We study formation and propagation in one contract economy. Contracts occupy a typed undirected network. Conditional on a regular agreement stratum, economically executable configurations form a manifold with corners. Parties choose legal architectures summarized by six functional channels. Agreement-compatible dynamics generate a forward-invariant productive region; reduction to a funding–technology observable yields a directed operator JT F = −R + W. Direction is therefore derived from the contract system after an observable is chosen. On the cooperative subclass W ≥ 0, the normalized amplification A = ρ(R−1W) separates locally stable productive operation from propagation fragility. Signed cross-effects instead admit an exact two-state determinant test and a conservative absolute-value comparison bound. Because A depends on the selected architecture, contract design moves the boundary. Privately optimal architectures generally do not internalize their marginal contribution to A. We characterize the resulting wedge and resilient redesigns that lower A while preserving productive function. We also give a rank condition for identifying the six channels and state conditional data requirements for applying it. This paper conducts no systematic filing audit and estimates neither the six-channel profile nor A; narrower implications remain testable with executed-contract or supervisory data.
