detail.abstract: Human systems of evaluation, pedagogy, and social policy are built on a persistent misunderstanding of statistical variance. When exceptional performance or social progress naturally regresses toward the mean, the human mind interprets this mathematical regularity as a causal event demanding intervention. This blind spot generates a structural trap: it falsely validates punitive, shaming responses to failure while obscuring the neutral-to-negative effects of volatile praise. Drawing on Daniel Kahneman's (2011) account of regression to the mean, Silvan Tomkins' (1962, 1963) theory of discrete affect, Donald Nathanson's (1992) Compass of Shame, and recent neurobiological work on the lateral habenula (LHb), this paper argues that the introduction of shame into a naturally fluctuating system triggers a survival response that maximizes internal inhibition, redirecting the performer from problem-solving toward mistake-avoidance. The paper closes by contrasting this punitive architecture with low-inhibition, interest-driven models of instruction, and by proposing that authentic progress requires raising the collective baseline rather than reacting to statistical peaks and troughs.

title: Adaptive Organisational Engineering: Bounded Adaptability as a Principle of Organisational Architecture

detail.title: Adaptive Organisational Engineering: Bounded Adaptability as a Principle of Organisational Architecture
detail.abstract:
Organisations must produce reliable value in the present while adapting to changing conditions, absorbing disruption, preserving coherence through growth, renewing their capabilities, and remaining viable beyond current leaders. Existing scholarship offers substantial insight into these requirements through organisation design, socio-technical systems, organisational learning, dynamic capabilities, ambidexterity, paradox, resilience, modularity, organisational identity, and succession research. These insights, however, are commonly developed through specialised theoretical conversations, leaving a whole-system design question: how should these organisational capacities be related and governed together? 

     This conceptual paper introduces Adaptive Organisational Engineering (AOE), an integrative organisation-design discipline concerned with the deliberate construction and continuing renewal of the architecture through which complex human systems produce outcomes. AOE proposes Bounded Adaptability as its governing design principle. The principle assigns relative stability to a limited boundary layer comprising purpose, protected commitments, governance, interfaces, critical standards, and defined outcomes, while preserving adaptability in methods, workflows, tools, internal structures, and local practices. AOE organises organisational design into seven interdependent pillars connected through value, protection-and-amplification, and renewal flows. Five propositions are developed concerning architectural patterning, bounded autonomy, system-owned capability, scalable coordination, and organisational continuity. The paper argues that sustainable organisational value depends not only on present performance but on whether the architecture producing that performance is reliable, adaptable, scalable, renewable, and durable across leadership generations.

title: Workload, sacrificed quality of care work, and workplace violence among nurses. A work environment perspective
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Workload, sacrificed quality of care work, and workplace violence among nurses. A work environment perspective
detail.abstract: Background : Workload and time pressure increase the risk of patient-initiated workplace violence. However, the mechanism through which workload influences workplace violence remains unclear. Moreover, understanding the interactions between workload and the work environment related factors is important to implement preventive measures.Objective : This study aimed to explore the relationship between workload and workplace violence by patient. In particular, we examined the mediating role of sacrificed quality of care work in this relationship. In addition, we sought to determine whether organizational resources (instrumental resources, autonomy, supervisor support and colleagues support) moderated the risk of exposure to workplace violence.Design:  A secondary analysis of cross-sectional French survey data was conducted.Participants:  The sample consisted of 1,329 nurses working in French hospitals.Methods: A hierarchical modeling approach and a mediation analysis were conducted to assess how workload affects the risk of workplace violence. Further, moderation analyses were conducted to assess the moderating effects of organizational resources. Finally, the data were analyzed using moderated mediation regressions with the PROCESS macro on SAS.Results:  Our findings confirmed that workload was positively related to workplace violence. Our study extended previous research by examining how workload relates to workplace violence. Sacrificed quality of care work fully mediated this relationship. Several organizational resources moderated the indirect relationship between workload and workplace violence through sacrificed quality of care work. In poor work environments, high workload was more strongly related to a decline in the quality of care provided, and subsequently to workplace violence.Conclusions:  This study supports the work environment hypothesis, showing that poor and stressful work environments provide fertile ground for patients’ aggressive behaviors. High workload clearly increases the risk of workplace violence. One of the originalities of this article is to documented that this effect can be largely attributed to a decline in the quality of care provided by nurses when they face high workloads and time pressure. Nevertheless, instrumental resources, job autonomy and supervisor support appeared to be viable protective factors.

detail.abstract:
This paper introduces the Cognitive-Architectural Imperative (CAI), a foundational thesis synthesizing Herbert Simon’s(1952) “common maps” and James Scott’s(1998) “legibility.” It posits that any governing intelligence will inherently shape its organization’s structure to become legible and optimizable within its own cognitive architecture. This principle explains historical organizational forms and provides a general framework for analyzing governor-organization relationships.

Applying the CAI to the age of AI yields the Neural Convergence Thesis (NCT). It conditionally predicts that if and when DNN-based AGI/ASI becomes a governing intelligence, it will act as a powerful catalyst, driving organizations to become cognitive extension of its cognitive architecture. This requires the governing AI to possess sufficient capacity for modeling and reconfiguration, coupled with a goal-aligned motivation that treats seamless organizational integration as a key instrumental sub-goal (Bostrom,2014). Under competitive pressure, this leads to perfect legibility and recursive self-optimization via “structural backpropagation,” potentially transitioning organizations from distributed cognitive systems into unified cognitive entities—a shift foreshadowed by Horaguchi’s(2025) “thinking organization.”

The CAI provides a unified lens for reinterpreting organizational history as a quest for legibility across successive cognitive paradigms, and for anticipating a future progression from ANI to ASI. This trajectory—from human-centric organization to AI-driven convergence—is not deterministic. Potent defeaters, including technological bottlenecks, regulatory containment, and enduring anthropocentric friction, and others could arrest this evolution. Absent these defeaters, the NCT culminates in the ASI era with organizations becoming autonomous cognitive entities, fundamentally shifting the primary unit of ethical risk from the individual to the emergent superintelligent collective.

title: What Actually Predicts Content Shareability in a Large Corpus of Published Articles

detail.title: What Actually Predicts Content Shareability in a Large Corpus of Published Articles
detail.abstract: Berger and Milkman's (2012) study of New York Times articles found that emotionally arousing contentpositive (awe) or negative (anger, anxiety)-is shared more than emotionally flat content. We test whether this arousal-driven virality pattern, and a related "clickbait gap" hypothesis (that a mismatch between a headline's emotional tone and an article's actual tone increases sharing), hold in a different, previously untested corpus: 38,463 articles published by Mashable, using the publicly available UCI Online News Popularity dataset. Using robust OLS regression on log(shares), we find a more complicated picture than either hypothesis predicts. A simple bivariate specification suggests sentiment extremity increases shares, replicating the qualitative spirit of the arousal hypothesis; but this does not survive a fuller specification controlling for how subjectiveopinionated versus factual-an article's writing style is. In the fuller model, valence shows a significant inverted-U relationship with shares (moderate positivity outperforms extremes), while the title-body "affect gap" shows no robust relationship with sharing. The most robust predictor of shares across every specification is global subjectivity-how opinionated and emotionally engaged the writing is, independent of its valence-a result that survives every control and robustness check. We discuss why under-specified virality models can reach the opposite conclusion from fuller ones, and what this means for applying single-outlet virality theories to new content domains.

title: Digital Sovereignty as a Transitional Strategy: The AI Deployment Phase in the United States, China, and the European Union

detail.title: Digital Sovereignty as a Transitional Strategy: The AI Deployment Phase in the United States, China, and the European Union
detail.abstract: Competition over the deployment of generative AI across organisations, labour processes, and value chains is intensifying. The deployment phase is the monetisation layer of the digital stack, and in the United States, China, and the European Union, ruling blocs are managing the transition to this phase through digital sovereignty doctrines. Digitalsovereignty scholarship divides into constructivist views, which interpret these doctrines as cultural expressions of authoritarian or liberal regimes, and materialist views, which regard them as protectionism or infrastructural territorialisation. Neither explains why formally distinct American, Chinese, and European digital doctrines converge on similar deployment-centric infrastructural reorganisations of capital accumulation. Recasting this divide through neo-Gramscian IPE, this article argues that digital sovereignty is the capitalist state's strategic-cultural form for managing this transition. It demonstrates how ruling blocs co-constitute the infrastructures and discourses essential to renewed accumulation, including "freedom" in the US and "counter-hegemony" in China. A conjunctural-comparative methodology traces how strategic-cultural formulations in Trump's AI Action Plan, Xi's New Quality Productive Forces, and Strengthening Europe's Tech Sovereignty authorise deployment-centric reorganisation around labour-force transition, state-capital integration, and extraterritorial market access. The article contributes to neo-Gramscian analysis by theorising strategic culture as a deliberate mediation between material restructuring and ideological articulation under capitalism.

title: Can We Fix Wasted Ad Spend by Re-ranking Users? Sure-Thing Penalized Uplift: A Study of What Works and What Doesn't
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Can We Fix Wasted Ad Spend by Re-ranking Users? Sure-Thing Penalized Uplift: A Study of What Works and What Doesn't
detail.abstract: When you run an ad campaign, a big chunk of your budget goes to users who would have bought anyway. They don't need the ad at all. In earlier work [3] we found that all of the standard models waste 86-92% of their targeting budget this way, and that better model accuracy doesn't fix it. This paper tests a natural fix: lower the score of users who already have a high chance of buying without the ad. We call this Sure-Thing Penalized Uplift (STPU). We tested two versions. Additive STPU subtracts a penalty from the score. Multiplicative STPU (MSTPU) multiplies the score by how much "room" the user has left to be influenced. Neither one works. Additive STPU made things worse every time we tried it. The reason turns out to be a simple numbers problem: the penalty we subtract is 2-5× larger in scale than the scores themselves, so the penalty takes over and we end up targeting the wrong people entirely. Multiplicative STPU fixes the scale problem but shows no consistent improvement across 567 experiments. It helped about as often as a coin flip. The deeper reason neither approach works is that at a 5% conversion rate, fewer than 7% of users actually benefit from an ad on any given day. Even a perfect model could only reduce budget waste to 78%, and the best real models sit at 86-92%. That remaining gap can't be closed by re-ranking, because there isn't enough signal in binary (yes/no) conversion data to reliably pick out those rare responsive users. Fixing budget waste requires richer data, such as revenue per user or multiple touchpoints per user. Smarter sorting of noisy binary signals won't get you there.

detail.abstract:
This paper tests whether changes in measured economic freedom cause development outcomes in Latin America rather than merely covary with them. The empirical object is a harmonized LATAM-11 country-year panel combining Economic Freedom of the World (EFW), the Heritage Index, World Development Indicators, the Worldwide Governance Indicators, Penn World Table 11.0, the Global Macro Database, and World Bank commodity prices. The analysis separates aggregate freedom, market-oriented policy, government size, state capacity, and state efficiency. It also expands the outcome space from growth, inequality, poverty, health, and productivity to mortality, alternative poverty thresholds, human capital, investment, trade, inflation, unemployment, education, health spending, taxation, government consumption, and state capability. Identification is deliberately triangulated. Baseline two-way fixed effects, long differences, five-year forward outcomes, local projections, synthetic controls, weak-IV diagnostics, leave-one-country-out tests, and specification curves are supplemented by abrupt-reform event designs based on isolated positive and negative changes, matched contemporaneous counterfactuals, nonnegative synthetic event controls, synthetic difference-indifferences , low-rank matrix-completion counterfactuals, event-year reassignment inference, pseudo-event dates, dependence-preserving circular shifts, leave-one-event-out deletion, threshold perturbations, random-component-index placebos, expanded sample restrictions, country-specific trends, temporal negative controls, event-definition grids, shock-timing predictability diagnostics, double/debiased machine learning with six nuisance-learning architectures and a Super Learner, machine-learning augmented inverse-probability weighting for abrupt shocks, R-learning for heterogeneous continuous effects, and T-, X-, DR-, and R-meta-learners for large positive and negative annual changes. The stronger battery, including 29 additional WDI mechanism outcomes and 145 additional outcome-by-driver tests, does not produce a stable causal coefficient for aggregate economic freedom. Some conventional or machine-learning specifications yield nominally significant coefficients, but they fail multiplicity, overlap, event-randomization, sign-stability, alternative-treatment, or alternative-counterfactual tests. Abrupt EFW rises and falls are especially informative because their post-event paths are not mirror images: apparent gains after falls and losses after rises coexist with small event counts and weak reassignment evidence. State capacity and efficiency occasionally produce suggestive signals, but the signs disagree across matched-event, DML, and AIPW designs. The central conclusion is therefore not that markets or states are irrelevant. It is that composite institutional indices are too heterogeneous and too endogenous to support a single causal development coefficient in this regional panel. The empirically defensible unit of policy analysis is the specific reform,
mechanism, implementation environment, and counterfactual.

detail.abstract: This paper replicates and extends Lee and Hoffman (2025) by replacing human participants with large language model (LLM) agents in a repeated Bertrand oligopoly with varied cheap talk frequencies. Three agents compete over 30 rounds in one of four configurations, a heterogeneous market (Claude Sonnet 4.6, GPT-4o, Gemini 2.5 Flash) and three homogeneous markets composed of three independent instances of a single model, across six communication frequency conditions, with 20 independent groups per cell (480 groups in total). We confirm two replication results: communication rounds yield higher prices than non-communication rounds in the heterogeneous and homogeneous-Gemini configurations, and all communication treatments exceed the no-communication baseline in every configuration. Two novel results emerge. First, the homogeneity coordination premium is model-specific rather than universal. Homogeneous Claude and Gemini markets price substantially above the heterogeneous market in all six treatments, including the nocommunication control, with a gap that is statistically constant across conditions; homogeneous GPT-4o markets are indistinguishable from the heterogeneous market in every treatment. Homogeneous Claude markets are the most collusive without communication: the three identical agents submit exactly identical prices in a majority of rounds, and in four of twenty no-communication groups prices ratchet upward in lockstep from 33 to nearly 90. Second, within the heterogeneous configuration, Gemini applies a systematic single-unit undercutting rule in 38.4 percent of rounds, generating a win rate of 96.1 percent against competitors with similar average submitted prices. An exploratory finding documents a rank reversal: every-other-round communication ranks first for human participants but last for LLM heterogeneous agents. These results imply that collusion risk in AI pricing markets depends on which models are deployed and whether competitors deploy the same one, not only on communication architecture or provider diversity.

detail.abstract:
Persistent instability in the Ghana Cedi to United States dollar exchange rate af-
fects inflation, trade, investment, and monetary policy in Ghana. This study looks
at the presence and effects of structural breaks in the exchange rate series. It evalu-
ates the forecasting performance of three modeling approaches: ARIMA, Prophet, and
Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM). The analysis aims to identify structural breaks,
determine their timing and nature, and assess how instabilities impact forecast ac-
curacy. Results from the Bai-Perron multiple structural break test and the Iterated
Cumulative Sum of Squares (ICSS) test confirm the existence of structural changes in
both the mean and volatility of the series. Further change point analysis using binary
segmentation identifies multiple shifts in the mean and variance, which align with ma-
jor macroeconomic shocks and monetary policy changes. Forecast evaluation shows
that the Prophet model outperformed the ARIMA and LSTM models, recording the lowest error measures (MAE = 1.80, MSE = 3.73, RMSE = 1.93) and producing more
accurate forecasts. Although the LSTM model displayed moderate predictive perfor-
mance, the ARIMA model performed relatively poorly. The findings emphasize the
need to consider structural breaks in exchange rate modeling and forecasting. They
also provide useful insights for policymakers, investors, and businesses in managing
exchange rate uncertainty and risk.

detail.abstract: Local government agencies in Indonesia are increasingly dependent on internally developed digital tools to support administrative workflows, yet the Software Quality Assurance (SQA) practices underpinning these tools remain under-documented in the academic literature, particularly for rolebased, low-resource public-sector environments. This paper presents a practice-based case study of the SQA process applied to APTIKATOOLS, an internal web application used by the Aplikasi dan Informatika (APTIKA) division of the West Java Provincial Communication and Informatics Office (Diskominfo) to manage correspondence, task assignment, and work reporting. Drawing on a structured, ten-stage QA workflow, spanning actor and role identification, role-based access control (RBAC) mapping, test-case design, black-box functional testing, bug reporting, and retesting, the study documents how quality assurance was operationalized in a real government IT environment and evaluates this practice against established SQA, software testing, and RBAC frameworks. A SWOT-TOWS analysis is used to synthesize internal capabilities and external conditions into actionable strategy. The findings indicate that the process's principal strengths lie in its traceable documentation and role-differentiated test design, while its central weaknesses are the absence of automated testing, standardized quality metrics, and centralized bug tracking, limitations that mirror capacity constraints frequently observed in digitalizing public-sector organizations. The paper contributes an empirically grounded account of how SQA and RBAC principles translate into practice within a resource-constrained government setting, and offers concrete recommendations, regression test suites, quality metrics, centralized bug tracking, standardized role matrices, and phased test automation for strengthening quality assurance maturity in similar institutional contexts.

detail.abstract: The relationship between patent delay and innovation has been widely studied in advanced economies, yet its implications in emerging innovation systems remain underexplored. This article examines the Brazilian case, where prolonged patent examination delays have historically functioned as a structural constraint rather than a purely strategic instrument. Drawing on the literature on patent systems, innovation economics, and institutional theory, the study argues that excessive delays in patent publication and grant undermine knowledge diffusion, increase market uncertainty, and weaken incentives for technological investment. Using a comprehensive dataset of 874,680 patent applications from the Brazilian National Institute of Industrial Property (INPI), this study employs Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) and multiple linear regression to investigate the structural determinants of patent prosecution delays. The findings reveal that the number of applicants (R² = 22.18%) and the technological sector (R² = 20.32%) are the primary explanatory factors, while temporal filing cohort (0.64%) and technological complexity (0.01%) have negligible effects. Patents with six or more applicants exhibit an average delay of approximately 5,455 additional days compared to single-applicant filings, whereas the 2020+ cohort shows a significant reduction of 530 days—evidence of institutional improvements. Recent reforms—particularly the Backlog Combat Plan introduced in 2019 and international cooperation mechanisms such as the Patent Prosecution Highway (PPH)—suggest a transition toward a more efficient and strategically navigable system. The analysis highlights a shift from systemic delay toward hybrid dynamics in which firms increasingly incorporate timing into their innovation strategies. The article contributes to the literature by positioning institutional efficiency as a central determinant of innovation outcomes in developing economies.

title: Infinite-Horizon Consumption Ratcheting under Epstein-Zin Preferences
affiliations: Kyung Hee University - Department of Applied Mathematics

detail.title: Infinite-Horizon Consumption Ratcheting under Epstein-Zin Preferences
detail.abstract: We solve an infinite-horizon consumption-investment problem with nondecreasing consumption under Epstein-Zin stochastic differential utility. Dynamic programming yields a two-state singular-control Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman variational inequality. Under an explicit single-crossing condition, homogeneity reduces the problem to a nonlinear free-boundary ordinary differential equation for the wealth-consumption ratio, whose regular singular solution corresponds to the unstable orbit of a hyperbolic saddle. A unique transverse crossing identifies the consumption trigger. We construct the reflected optimal policy and verify its optimality using recursive-utility comparison and an exact transversality estimate. As the inverse elasticity of intertemporal substitution approaches relative risk aversion, preferences converge to the time-additive constant-relative-riskaversion case, and the solution converges to Dybvig's ratcheting benchmark.

title: The Riemann Ξ-Function as a Characteristic Function
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Riemann Ξ-Function as a Characteristic Function

keywords: Linnik Provide your feedback on BizChat

detail.abstract:
We survey the probabilistic reformulations of the Riemann Hypothesis (RH) that are organised around the Riemann Ξ-function, and we assess what part of this circle of ideas is legitimately attributable to Yu. V. Linnik. The narrow answer is negative: there is no Linnik theorem about Ξ; the reality-of-zeros programme runs Pólya → Turán → de Bruijn → Newman → Rodgers-Tao. The broad answer is affirmative and, we argue, more useful. Linnik's two legacies-(i) the unconditional substitutes for RH and GRH (the large sieve, log-free zero-density estimates, the Deuring-Heilbronn repulsion phenomenon, Linnik's identity, the dispersion method), and (ii) the theory of entire characteristic functions, ridge functions, and the Linnik-Ostrovskii arithmetic of probability laws-together supply exactly the language in which the modern van Dantzig and Laguerre-Pólya reformulations of RH are stated. 

     We then push the probabilistic reading one step further. Writing X Ξ for the symmetric random variable with characteristic function φ(t) = Ξ(t)/Ξ(0), we record two structural facts. First, X Ξ is never infinitely divisible, because φ has zeros; the infinite-divisibility question therefore belongs not to X Ξ but to its van Dantzig partner Y Ξ , whose characteristic function is Ξ(0)/Ξ(it). Second-and this is the organising observation of the paper-RH is equivalent to the statement that Y Ξ is an infinite convolution of symmetric Laplace laws with scales 1/γ, γ running over the positive ordinates of the zeta zeros. Equivalently, Y Ξ lies in the Thorin class T (R) of extended generalized gamma convolutions with Thorin measure equal to the zero-counting measure, U = γ>0 δ γ. The Lévy density of Y Ξ is |x|-1 γ>0 e-γ|x| , whose evaluation by the Weil explicit formula converts the Thorin measure into a sum over primes. We give a cumulant-alternation criterion and verify it numerically through order twenty. 

     The converse question-whether positive-definiteness of the partner's candidate characteristic function is by itself equivalent to RH-we settle partially. Writing ψ as a signed mixture of Laplace laws with weights summing to one, we prove via Landau's theorem for Laplace transforms of nonnegative functions that positive-definiteness forces the zeros of least ordinate onto the critical line, and no more; exact high-precision computation of the mixture density shows that displacing any higher zero off the line, even to the edge of the critical strip, leaves the density nonnegative. The van Dantzig criterion is therefore a consequence of RH worth exploiting rather than a route to proving it. Applying a Lévy-to-Thorin lemma at the centre α = 1 2 , where the drift vanishes because ξ ′ (1 2) = 0, identifies the partner as a Gaussian variance mixture √ 2H Z and separates two hypotheses that are easily conflated: the existence of H pins only the lowest zero, whereas H being a generalized gamma convolution is equivalent to RH. The arithmetic input is exactly Λ ≥ 0, carried by a sine-squared transform.

title: Thorin Quantisation
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Thorin Quantisation
detail.abstract: The reciprocal of a normalised Laguerre-Pólya entire function is the Laplace transform of a generalised gamma convolution (GGC) whose Thorin measure is supported on the squared zeros. We show that for entire functions of genus zero the converse holds in a strong form: if the associated clock is a GGC at all, its Thorin measure is automatically a counting measure with unit atoms. Quantisation is therefore not an extra hypothesis but a consequence, and the entire content of the Riemann Hypothesis, read through the van Dantzig-Wald dictionary, sits in the single step from infinite divisibility to the Thorin class. We make this precise in three ways. First, we identify the GGC locus inside the class of van Dantzig solutions constructed by Konstantopoulos, Patie and Sarkar from Laplace exponents of spectrally negative Lévy processes: their hitting-time clocks are always selfdecomposable, and are GGC exactly when the associated entire function has only real zeros; the Mittag-Leffler instances give explicit self-decomposable hitting times that are not GGC. Second, we show that no Lévy-Khintchine representation of log ξ(α + s) with a non-negative Lévy measure can be established at α = 1 2 without already assuming the absence of zeros to the right of α, and we correct a spurious Thorin atom that arises when ξ is factored through the pole of ζ. Third, working from the shifted basepoint s = 3 2 , we prove that RH is equivalent to σ → ξ(3 2)/ξ(1 2 + √ 1 + σ) being the Laplace transform of a GGC, equivalently to its hyperbolic complete monotonicity, and we convert this into a determinantal criterion: RH holds if and only if the Hankel matrices of the power sums c n = ρ [(3 2-ρ)(ρ + 1 2)]-(n+1) , summed over zero pairs, are positive semidefinite. The criterion is unconditionally computable from the Taylor coefficients of ξ at 3 2 ; we verify it numerically through order five and recover γ 1 = 14.1347. .. from the coefficient ratios.

detail.abstract:
This paper investigates the integration of climate transition risk into quantitative factor investing on the Johannesburg Stock Exchange (JSE). We engineer a novel "Climate-Resilient" long-short factor portfolio by sorting listed firms based on their implied climate sensitivity (λ), derived from carbon emission intensities, asset life cycle exposures, and regulatory transition costs. The strategy takes a long position in low-λ (climate-resilient) firms and a short position in high-λ (transition-vulnerable) firms. Backtesting results over the 2018-2026 period demonstrate an enhanced Sharpe ratio, controlled portfolio turnover, and robust execution capacity within the liquidity constraints of emerging African markets. 

     The motivation for this study stems from two converging trends. First, South Africa's energy matrix remains heavily dependent on coal, exposing listed firms to regulatory, technological, and reputational transition shocks. Second, global institutional capital is increasingly reallocating toward climate-aware mandates, creating systematic mispricing for firms that fail to adapt. By quantifying transition risk at the firm level and embedding it into a tradable factor, this paper provides an implementable framework for investors seeking to hedge climate exposure while capturing alpha. 

     Our empirical findings suggest that climate sensitivity is a priced risk factor on the JSE. The long-short portfolio generates 3.7% annual excess return over the benchmark with 1.7% lower volatility. Importantly, the strategy maintains semi-annual turnover below 45% and estimated capacity above ZAR 4.5 billion, indicating that climate-resilient investing is not only academically interesting but also practically viable in an emerging market context.

title:
The Formula of Capital:
Ontology and Theoretical Unification of Economics

detail.title:
The Formula of Capital:
Ontology and Theoretical Unification of Economics
detail.abstract:
This article proposes a labor value theory articulated through one unified equality. This equality is neither a technical model nor an accounting identity. It is an ontology. It provides the structure to understand why value exists, why it is destroyed, accumulated, enters into crisis, inflated, validated, or denied. 
The formula reveals the dialectical origin of macroeconomic phenomena through the common variables (omega and pi), since the same social structure organizes both production and realization, making it possible to distinguish between the phenomenon and its dual cause. This turns the formula into a unique tool—an ontological framework for comprehending the social totality of capitalism, with which dynamic simulations, econometric dashboards, and new theoretical explorations can be developed. 
The equality thus becomes a bridge between the ontology of labor value and contemporary research practice. This preprint highlights the formula as a concise entry point, making theoretical unification accessible to a broader academic audience and ensuring proper citation of the complete work.

detail.title: Beyond Tariff Preferences: Rules of Origin and the Legal Architecture of African Economic Integration under the AfCFTA
detail.abstract:
The African Continental Free Trade Area (AfCFTA) is intended to boost trade among African countries and to improve economic integration throughout the continent.One of the key ways in which it aims to do this is by means ofpreferential tariff treatment for products exchanged between State Parties. 


The benefits of these preferences are dependent on the ability to establsh whether a product is eligible as originating in the AfCFTA. This article examines why these rules are important to the operation of the AfCFTA preferential regime. It argues that their role is not limited to determining which goods qualify for preferential treatment. They also protect the value of the preferences by preventing goods originating outside Africa from obtaining them through trade deflection. At the same time, rules of origin can influence where businesses source materials and organise production, particularly through continental cumulation, and can therefore contribute to the development of African value chains. The article argues that the effectiveness of the AfCFTA rules of origin depends on maintaining a workable balance between these two functions. Rules that are too weak may undermine the preferential regime, while rules that are too restrictive or costly to comply with may discourage African producers from using the preferences available to them. The article therefore considers the rules of origin not simply as technical customs requirements, but as an important part of the legal framework through which the AfCFTA seeks to promote greater economic integration and value addition within Africa.

title: Europe’s Climate Ambition Under Scrutiny: Evidence from Deep Learning Emission Projections
affiliations: Polytechnic University of Milan, RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment, RFF-CMCC European Institute on Economics and the Environment and Polytechnic University of Milan

detail.title: Europe’s Climate Ambition Under Scrutiny: Evidence from Deep Learning Emission Projections
detail.abstract: The European Union has committed to reducing greenhouse gas emissions 55\% below 1990 levels by 2030, but whether current trends are compatible with this ambition remains uncertain. We apply deep learning to high-resolution socioeconomic and sectoral data across EU27 member states till 2023 to project sectoral CO$_2$ trajectories under current trends, extrapolating observed sectoral momentum without assuming changes in the pace or effectiveness of the policy environment beyond what is already reflected in historical data. We project that EU27 emissions will exceed the 2030 target by 35\% (620 Mt CO$_2$ shortfall), with only a small minority of countries on trajectories consistent with the bloc's commitments. While the Power sector achieves target-consistent reductions driven by the renewable transition, Mobility shows minimal progress and accounts for over a third of total emissions by 2030, reflecting a structural inertia across member states rather than geographically concentrated lag. Our findings indicate that substantial additional intervention is required to close Europe's ambition-implementation gap, and call for establishing up-to-date energy information in Europe.

detail.abstract: Biophysical economics has framed the limits to growth in terms of two low-entropy sources: the terrestrial mineral stock and the solar flow. This paper argues for a third, analytically distinct source: human time and builds the accounting it requires. Extending Georgescu-Roegen's flow-fund model, we specify the time-fund as a hybrid the original taxonomy lacks: a fund whose non-storable services are continuously reproduced through low-entropy throughput, yet which dissipates at a fixed rate whether used or not. We define entropic rent (R) as the exergy appropriated through human hours net of the reproduction cost of those hours, and time capitalization (κ) as the exergy mobilized per appropriated hour. Applied to the information and AI economy, the framework predicts that dematerialization relocates dissipation rather than removing it, and that a stalling κ is compensated by an expanding claim on unwaged hours. A pilot implementation for the United States, 1900-2024, carries the accounting from statement to measurement. Measured on waged hours, useful work per hour plateaus after 1973; measured on all appropriated hours, the denominator the framework specifies, it falls by 38 per cent, while the appropriated share of the time-fund (α) rises from 0.33 to 0.49an increase located entirely outside the wage relation. The unwaged margin is calibrated rather than measured, and the boundary between reproduction and appropriation moves R three times more than every measurement term combined. Four propositions state the framework in refutable form.

detail.abstract: Why do otherwise similar firms differ in their ability to convert technological opportunities into innovation? This paper studies whether one explanation lies in CEO prior exposure to innovation at other firms where they previously served on boards. Linking BoardEx employment histories to USPTO AI patents, we construct grant-based measures of CEO external AI innovation exposure. Firms led by CEO with greater external AI innovation exposure subsequently produce more AI Innovation, robust to firm, CEO and industry-year controls, and the relation is specific to AI rather than general patenting. Event studies around CEO turnover, comparing firms with similar pre-turnover innovation potential, show that the arrival of exposed CEO is followed by increases in both AI Innovation Filings and AI Innovation, with no evidence of pre-existing filing trends. The effect is stronger in firms with greater absorptive capacity, and exposed insider and outsider CEO transitions have similar effects. Exposed CEO are also associated with the reallocation of AI inventors to the firm, including from firms on whose boards they previously served, and give rise to first-time AI inventors at the firm. The findings show that technology-specific CEO exposure is a form of managerial human capital that helps firms transform frontier technological opportunities into realized innovation.

detail.abstract: Empirical evidence suggests that women, on average, are employed in lesscarbon-intensive sectors compared to men and exhibit stronger support forclimate action. The analysesrely on numerical experiments within an Environmental Dynamic StochasticGeneral Equilibrium (E-DSGE) model in which men and women differ in theirpreferences over carbon-intensive goods and in their comparative advantageacross sectors. title: Conjugate Bayesian Inference for Generalised Waring Distributions
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: Conjugate Bayesian Inference for Generalised Waring Distributions
detail.abstract: The generalised Waring distribution GW(a, k; ρ) is the canonical model for accident and repeatevent counts, since it decomposes overdispersion into components attributable to randomness, proneness and liability. Its likelihood is a ratio of Pochhammer symbols in all three parameters, and this has kept full Bayesian inference out of reach. We provide a conjugate analysis. Our approach introduces a reciprocal gamma prior, the density proportional to a reciprocal Pochhammer symbol, which is the natural conjugate object for the gamma ratios appearing in the likelihood. We then construct a Pólya-Gamma style data augmentation scheme: a beta latent variable linearises the Pochhammer symbol in the denominator into an exponential tilt, and a Chinese restaurant table latent variable linearises the Pochhammer symbol in the numerator into a power. Conditional on the two latents, all three parameters have gamma or reciprocal gamma complete conditionals, and the sampler is a three-block Gibbs scheme with no Metropolis steps and no tuning. For the Waring sub-family with k = 1 we obtain the marginal posterior in closed form as a finite sum of residues, and we verify this representation to 120 digits. We also establish a fact that conditions any Bayesian treatment of this model. The GW likelihood is exactly symmetric under a ↔ k, so a and k are individually unidentified: only ρ and symmetric functions of (a, k) are estimable. Marginal posteriors for a and k are therefore bimodal, and the slow mixing reported for this model is a symptom of the symmetry rather than of the algorithm. We report inference for identified functionals throughout. We show that the conditional for the tail parameter is log-concave, so the sampler is exact without augmentation, and that the identification failure is confined to the intercept-only, single-period case: covariates break the symmetry, and so does replication. With J = 300 individuals observed T = 5 times each, proneness and liability separate cleanly, whereas at T = 1 they do not. The reason is transparent in the bivariate model, where the cross-margin covariance is shown to equal the proneness component of the variance exactly, annihilating the randomness and liability components. Covariates break the symmetry too, and conditionally on the two latent variables the regression likelihood is exactly that of a Poisson log-linear model, so a generalised Waring regression is no harder to fit than a Poisson one. Applied to the Greenwood and Yule accident data, the posterior places essentially all mass on ρ > 2, and attributes roughly 47% of the variance to randomness, with the remainder split between liability and proneness in a ratio the single-period counts cannot determine.

title: New Green Alliances: Requirements to Implement Long-run International Sustainable Energy Partnerships
affiliations: RWTH Aachen University and RWTH Aachen University

detail.title: New Green Alliances: Requirements to Implement Long-run International Sustainable Energy Partnerships
detail.abstract: International renewable energy partnerships are increasingly promoted to enhance energy security, accelerate decarbonization, and mobilize private capital for large-scale cross-border infrastructure. Their long-run viability, however, depends on whether cooperation between heterogeneous governments and private investors is incentive-compatible under realistic market and policy conditions. This paper develops a tripartite evolutionary game-theoretical model to analyze the dynamic stability of international sustainable energy partnerships. The framework captures strategic interaction between energy-importing governments, energy-exporting governments, and private sector investors, with payoffs incorporating net present values of infrastructure investments, carbon pricing, transaction costs, and alternative public–private partnership remuneration schemes. The model is calibrated to a prospective renewable hydrogen partnership between the European Union and North African countries and used to examine how energy prices, levelized production costs, capital costs, and institutional design parameters affect equilibrium selection. The results show that under incomplete pricing of environmental externalities, private investment is not incentive-compatible at scale. Improvements in technology costs or energy prices alone are insufficient to generate dynamically stable cooperation. Instead, institutional design critically shapes long-run outcomes. In particular, joint public co-investment reduces asymmetric windfall gains and strengthens governments’ commitment incentives, while availability-based public–private partnerships improve private risk allocation and enhance stability relative to concession models. The findings highlight that the success of international sustainable energy partnerships depends less on technological progress alone than on incentive-compatible institutional design and coordinated public investment structures.

title: An Optimal Energy Production Problem with Energy Source Switching and Load Following Nuclear Power Plants
