detail.title: An Optimal Energy Production Problem with Energy Source Switching and Load Following Nuclear Power Plants
detail.abstract: The integration of weather-dependent renewable generation increases the volatility of residual demand and raises the value of dispatchable low-carbon flexibility. This paper studies the optimal operation of a load-following nuclear power plant owned by a producer that must balance stochastic residual demand while accounting for ramping limits and costly changes in operating regimes. Nuclear output can be increased, decreased, or kept constant, and the production decision is formulated as a finite-horizon optimal switching problem. We analyze both a closed-economy benchmark, where excess production cannot be sold and shortages require costly back-up generation, and an open-economy setting, where the producer can trade electricity at prices driven by aggregate market residual demand. The value functions are characterized as viscosity solutions of a system of Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman quasi-variational inequalities, and optimal policies are computed using a monotone semi-Lagrangian scheme. The numerical results show how shortage costs, switching costs, ramping capability, and market access shape optimal nuclear load following. The analysis highlights the economic value of controllable low-carbon capacity in renewable-intensive systems and provides implications for flexibility remuneration, balancing-market design, and interconnection policy.

title: The Thorin Measure of the Riemann Zeta Function
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business

detail.title: The Thorin Measure of the Riemann Zeta Function
detail.abstract: The completed Riemann zeta function, read as a function of v = s(1-s), is entire of order one half and so has a Hadamard product of genus zero. Its zero measure U ζ , the pushforward of the zeros under ρ → ρ(1-ρ), is a Thorin measure, equivalently 1/(2Ω(-s)) is the Laplace transform of a generalised gamma convolution, precisely when the Riemann hypothesis holds. The defect from Thorin's class is then not an obstruction but a number, the Krein-Langer index κ, and we prove a signature count showing that κ is exactly the number of negative eigenvalues of the associated Hankel matrices, and that these are built from the cumulants of the underlying gamma convolution. A recent paper attributed to a large language model developed at Anthropic proves unconditionally that at least 2 3 of the zeros of ζ in a dyadic window lie on the critical line, that at least 2 3 are simple and on the line, and that at least 5 6 are distinct. Translated: at least two thirds of the localised Thorin mass is carried by the positive real axis, at least two thirds of it consists of unit atoms, and the Krein-Langer defect is at most one sixth, against seven twenty-fourths from the previous unconditional record. The mechanism of that proof, a finite compression of Weil's Hermitian form together with two trace moments, Sylvester's law of inertia and a rank-trace inequality, is the indefinite truncated Stieltjes moment problem for the same measure. We record the dictionary, identify where it is exact and where it fails, compare it with Li's criterion, note a reading of the certificate in terms of effective dimension familiar from shrinkage, and set out twelve open problems. An appendix records an independent check of every constant asserted here, including four errors it turned up in our own first draft.

title: Incentives to Expand Transmission Capacity for Cross-Border Electricity Trade in Europe
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, University of Groningen, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Incentives to Expand Transmission Capacity for Cross-Border Electricity Trade in Europe
detail.abstract: To what extent are incentives to expand transmission capacity for cross-border electricity trade aligned between countries? We address this question within the context of realizing the vision of a climate-neutral Europe by 2050. We compare two scenarios using a large-scale optimization model of the European electricity system (COMPETES). The first is based on the projected transmission capacity for 2030 (Base Grid); the second the capacity optimized for 2050 (Expanded Grid).We find that the expansion of transmission capacity reduces average electricity prices by 2.7% in 2050, but that the benefits are unevenly distributed. Transmission expansion stimulates renewable investment in the periphery and discourages nuclear investment across Europe: in Norway, offshore wind capacity increases sevenfold; in Spain, solar capacity doubles. Yet where prices in Spain fall by 14%, they rise by 19% in Norway. This country-level misalignment — Norway hosts more generation capacity yet faces higher prices — may hinder efficient transmission expansion and Europe achieving its decarbonization goals.

title: Measuring 5G+ Broadband Networks -Emerging Technical and Policy Challenges
affiliations: , affiliation not provided to SSRN, Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (CSAIL), Universidad Politécnica de Madrid, Technische Universität Berlin (TU Berlin) and University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB)

detail.title: Measuring 5G+ Broadband Networks -Emerging Technical and Policy Challenges
detail.abstract: 5G and beyond (5G+) networks promise to support a broad range of heterogeneous services, from enhanced mobile broadband (eMBB) to ultra-reliable low-latency communications (URLLC) and massive IoT. Realizing this promise depends on the ability of ecosystem stakeholders (mobile network operators, regulators, content/application providers, and end-users) to make evidence-based decisions, which in turn, requires meaningful measurements. However, collecting, interpreting, and comparing relevant data is complex. Answering pressing entrepreneurial and policy questions requires multiple metrics from multiple vantage points. This paper makes the case for a multi-stakeholder measurement ecosystem for 5G+ networks, examining how technical, economic, and governance challenges translate into measurement needs. We assess and compare the predominant measurement methodologies (unattended probes, drive tests, and crowdsourced approaches), analyzing their trade-offs in controllability, spatio-temporal resolution, scalability, cost, and data trustworthiness. We show how contextual factors, including indoor versus outdoor environments, device heterogeneity, and environmental conditions, fundamentally challenge metric interpretability, and how the coexistence of "competing" definitions and metrics for 5G and service performance and measurement approaches yield divergent coverage and performance assessments, posing additional challenges for policymaking. We conclude by reviewing emerging measurement paradigms and derive implications for evidence-based broadband policy. Those include hybrid data collection via UAV and satellite vantage points; and, AI/ML-driven analytics such as NWDAF-enabled data fusion and predictive optimization.

title: Introducing Economic Disparity and Housing Immobility to Schelling's Dynamic Model of Segregation

detail.title: Introducing Economic Disparity and Housing Immobility to Schelling's Dynamic Model of Segregation

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding

detail.abstract: Drawing on Thomas Schelling's 1971 dynamic model of racial segregation, this paper reexamines the model by introducing economic constraints that reflect modern limitations on wealth-driven sorting. Though Schelling's model effectively introduces segregation patterns influenced by social preference, it fails to account for real-world housing market patterns driven by financial mobility. To bridge said gap, the standard model was modified to mimic a city scaled by property values based on proximity to the geometrical center, with two agent groups assigned varying degrees of income disparity. As a result, this introduced an agent state of "trapped," in which the agent's desire to relocate based on social preference is inhibited by a lack of purchasing power. Running 2000 simulations across a control group and three economic disparity levels (low, medium and high) with varying social preference thresholds, the model deduces three key findings: (1) Income disparity drove spatial economic sorting, (2) interestingly, increased income disparity reduced overall social segregation by inhibiting feedback loops based on social preference, and (3) high income disparity led to housing friction which made 12% of agents "trapped." Ultimately, these findings suggest that economic disparity successfully influences segregation patterns and, crucially, incorporates financial constraints into urban sociological models.

title: Implications of the EU CBAM on Ukraine’s economy and environment
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Purdue University, Department of Agricultural Economics, affiliation not provided to SSRN and National Academy of Sciences of Ukraine

detail.title: Implications of the EU CBAM on Ukraine’s economy and environment
detail.abstract: The European Union’s (EU) Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM) began its paid phase in 2026. As exporters adjust to new regulations, many EU trading partners are concerned with the potential implications of the CBAM for their economies. Ukraine is one of the key EU’s trading partners with substantial exports of the CBAM-covered commodities, particularly steel. Despite being highly-exposed to the CBAM policy, potential impacts CBAM on Ukraine have not been comprehensively assessed. In this paper we address this research gap by relying on a global multi-region input-output database (GTAP-CE) with detailed representation of the CBAM-covered products and couple it with a global recursive-dynamic computable general equilibrium model ENVISAGE. Using this methodological framework, we analyse the impacts of various CBAM implementations on Ukraine, also taking into account impacts of the war and the expected post-war recovery efforts. Results indicate that CBAM induces modest but targeted structural adjustments. Carbon-intensive sectors, especially iron and steel and energy, contract slightly, while cleaner and non-CBAM sectors expand due to factor reallocation. Trade effects are more pronounced than output effects, with declines in exports of CBAM-covered goods such as steel and electricity, though aggregate exports remain largely unchanged. At the macro level, impacts are limited: GDP and welfare losses remain below 0.1%, while emissions decline modestly (up to ~0.8%), suggesting only marginal improvements in carbon intensity. Sensitivity analysis highlights that outcomes depend strongly on CBAM design, with inclusion of indirect (Scope 2) emissions generating substantially larger negative impacts, particularly for steel exports.

title: Observational Equivalence and Unilateral Strategic Feasibility under Coarse Monitoring

detail.title: Observational Equivalence and Unilateral Strategic Feasibility under Coarse Monitoring
detail.abstract: Coarse monitoring can make many action profiles observationally equivalent. This fact alone, however, does not determine which of those profiles a single privately informed agent can strategically reach. This paper isolates that distinction in a two-agent environment with decentralized information and aggregate monitoring. Each agent privately observes one component of a binary state. Exact state-contingent implementation requires the agents to use one another's information, while the monitor observes only the sum of their actions. The resulting zero-aggregate monitoring fiber is a continuum and contains the targets associated with both joint states. We show that this large observational-equivalence class has a sharply smaller unilateral strategic intersection. Holding the other agent to the prescribed decentralized strategy, a unilateral false report switches the counterparty's prescribed action to the action associated with the opposite genuine state. Conditional on preserving the monitored aggregate, the deviator then has a unique feasible completion. Consequently, the set of nontrivial monitor-preserving outcomes that one agent can unilaterally reach is a singleton: the target associated with the opposite joint state. Under a benchmark payoff specification with strictly positive losses from true-state action mismatch and monitored aggregate inconsistency, truthful decentralized behavior forms a pure-strategy ex post Nash equilibrium. An extension introducing a private rent from successfully realizing the concealed false-state allocation yields a sharp threshold: manipulation is unprofitable below the true-state mismatch loss, payoff-equivalent at equality, and profitable above it. The analysis separates the geometry of observational equivalence from the strategic geometry of unilateral concealed feasibility.

title: Composition of Quadratic Forms, Superposition, and Depth: Gauss, Cohen-Lenstra and Kolmogorov-Arnold
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and George Mason University

detail.title: Composition of Quadratic Forms, Superposition, and Depth: Gauss, Cohen-Lenstra and Kolmogorov-Arnold
detail.abstract: Gauss asked in 1801 for the length of the cycle produced by repeated composition of a binary quadratic form. The question is equivalent to the order of a class in the ideal class group and no exact rule exists. Cohen and Lenstra replaced it by an averaged question, and the recent work of Landesman and Levy repairs a withdrawn proof of the function field case and then delivers function field versions of the Malle and Poonen-Rains conjectures. We give a self contained account of the arithmetic and then develop a second theme. A quadratic form is exactly a one hidden layer network with square activation, minimal width equal to the rank, and the polynomial generalisation is Waring decomposition, where minimal width is symmetric tensor rank. Gauss composition and the Kolmogorov-Arnold superposition theorem then have a common shape: a multivariate operation becomes addition after univariate re-coordinatisation. Both are existence results whose univariate coordinates resist use, in one case because they cannot be made smooth and in the other because they are discrete logarithms. Reading iteration as depth, Gauss's riddle asks when iterated composition saturates, and Cohen-Lenstra answers the averaged version. We separate the exact statements from the structural parallels and state where the analogy fails. Working the resulting problems, we show that Dirichlet composition on concordant forms has Waring rank exactly two, so that Gauss composition is a width two square activation network with two skip connections, and that with Bezout data the general composite has rank at most eight. The arithmetic difficulty therefore lies entirely in the normalisation layer and not in the nonlinearity. We also show that Cayley's hyperdeterminant of the Bhargava cube is the discriminant, so that the real versus imaginary dichotomy governing the two Cohen-Lenstra moment formulas coincides with the real tensor rank two versus rank three dichotomy.

title: Intervention, Not Inference: The Identification of Algorithmic Collusion

detail.title: Intervention, Not Inference: The Identification of Algorithmic Collusion
detail.abstract: Q-learning pricing agents sustain supra-competitive prices in simulation. Whether econometrics can detect such conduct is a separate question, and we answer it in a laboratory where the truth is known by construction: we reproduce Calvano et al. (2020), embed the agents in demand-shifting markets, and grade every method against three regimes of sharply differing true conduct. Detection requires intervention. Mandating a one-week price displacement by one firm and watching the rival yields, from a single market, what passive data never give: five probes detect a rival response with 83% power at a correctly-sized test, against 52% false positives passively, and response depth separates punishment from myopia at AUC 0.96. Direction matters more than the statistic. Since prices are strategic complements, a static best-responder must follow a rival's mandated increase at every marginal cost-the unobservable that defeats every passive method here-so a firm that cuts instead cannot be best-responding at any cost. That sign test separates punishment from a benign menu-cost defendant perfectly (AUC 1.00) under an exact paired counterfactual. Its null is narrow, though: it falsifies static best response, not competition, and memoryless learners, which cannot punish at all, violate it in 51% of markets. The passive toolkit fails instructively: it measures policy effects essentially perfectly-a randomized tax and a transparency mandate, with clean pre-trends and correct inferencebut cannot recover conduct. The collusive path is rationalizable, period by period, as static best response under an unrestricted cost process, so identification rests entirely on what may be assumed about costs. Conduct tests on the estimable transition are uninformative though the same test on an unobservable steady state would work; endogenous adoption defeats modern staggered estimators, a ladder of designs locating the failure in positivity rather than in outcome-dependence; and a screen with 99% held-out accuracy flags benign menu-cost competitors as collusive in 97% of out-of-taxonomy markets. Restricting costs to a constant does yield a genuine identified set-the grid best-response inequalities are linear in cost-recovering known costs to 0.001 and rejecting the collusive panel in every market. But it fails as the sign test does, measuring the precision of optimization rather than the objective-myopic and memoryless learners are rejected just as decisively. Punishment proves a property of the pricing stack, not of prices: it dissolves under function approximation while prices stay high, unmoved by a 32-fold sweep of the training budget. Conduct evidence, in short, has to be manufactured rather than found-and the intervention that works is the one whose null holds for every cost.

title: The African AI Enclave: Generative AI and the Modern Sector
affiliations: Central Bank of Nigeria

detail.title: The African AI Enclave: Generative AI and the Modern Sector
detail.abstract: Does generative AI diffuse broadly through African economies, or does it enter through the narrow modern sector? This paper provides new multi-country evidence on the occupational, purpose-of-use, and spatial incidence of observed generative-AI activity in Africa. Using Anthropic's Economic Index, I map Claude.ai conversations to occupational tasks across 22 African countries and weight them by model-estimated task time. I triangulate these patterns with OpenAI Signals and Google Gemini: ChatGPT independently corroborates both the crosscountry intensity gradient and the writing-and-technical tilt of African consumer use, while Gemini provides qualitative evidence of similar white-collar and educational concentration. A 24-month ChatGPT panel further shows that consumer use broadens over time, but significantly more slowly in African markets. Generative-AI activity is highly concentrated in professional-type tasks. In Kenya, occupations employing 3.5 percent of workers account for 95 percent of estimated task-time savings-a representation ratio of 27, compared with 3.6 in the United States. Activity also maps disproportionately to occupations with substantially lower informality rates than the workforce overall. Yet Africa is not exceptional: within a 60-country comparison sample, occupational concentration is statistically indistinguishable from that of non-African economies at comparable income levels. The enclave is therefore characteristic of early consumer-AI activity in lower-income economies. This occupational structure is persistent across comparable sampled weeks and survives disclosure-censoring checks. Where concentration declines in later, methodologically distinct releases, much of the movement remains within managerial and professional occupations rather than spreading into the jobs employing most workers. Coursework is as professionally concentrated as workplace use, while personal use is the least concentrated margin. Spatially, activity is highly concentrated relative to population, but comparisons with regional output and nighttime lights show that much of this pattern follows the pre-existing geography of modern economic activity. These patterns reveal a development divide within adoption: frontier AI access is expanding, but its observed task footprint remains anchored in the professional, relatively formal, and spatially concentrated modern sector rather than diffusing through the broader employment structure.

title: Patterns in 2026 Energy Markets
affiliations: University of British Columbia

detail.title: Patterns in 2026 Energy Markets
detail.abstract:
The 2026 energy market is being shaped by the intersection of geopolitical disruption, shifting investment priorities, and an accelerating transformation of the global energy system. At the center of this outlook is the Strait of Hormuz, whose prolonged disruption has emerged as the most significant source of uncertainty for oil and liquefied natural gas markets. With a substantial share of global oil and LNG flows dependent on the strait, the duration of the crisis will play a decisive role in determining energy prices, inflationary pressures, economic growth, and market performance through the remainder of 2026.

This report examines developments across oil and refined products, natural gas, coal, renewables, and nuclear power, while assessing the consequences for global investment and equity markets. Despite elevated fossil-fuel risks, structural investment continues to shift toward electricity generation, infrastructure, renewables, and nuclear capacity, reflecting growing electrification and rising power demand, including from AI data centres. At the same time, energy equities have substantially outperformed the broader market, particularly in upstream production, refining, and midstream activities, as geopolitical scarcity and higher commodity prices strengthen selected segments of the sector.

Three scenarios for the Strait of Hormuz—a rapid reopening, a negotiated summer settlement, and an extended disruption through the end of 2026—illustrate the wide range of potential outcomes. The analysis concludes that geopolitics is likely to dominate short-term energy-market dynamics, while electrification, renewable expansion, nuclear investment, and infrastructure development remain the principal structural forces reshaping the energy economy over the longer term.

title: Estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effects through Multilevel Modeling
affiliations: Auckland University of Technology, Auckland University of Technology, University of Economics Ho Chi Minh City and Ohio State University (OSU)

detail.title: Estimating Heterogeneous Treatment Effects through Multilevel Modeling
detail.abstract: We develop a multilevel (hierarchical) framework for event studies and demonstrate that the average treatment effect on the treated can be recovered directly from nested random-intercept structures, providing an alternative identification route to standard Difference-inDifferences estimators. Within this framework, we further derive a decomposition of heterogeneous treatment effects into a homogeneous component and a component driven by systematic differences in outcomes across treated units. This representation also implies that commonly used pretrend test may be misleading in the presence of treatment heterogeneity, as they fail to capture the effects of cross-unit outcome heterogeneity. We further show that the Difference-inDifferences using two-way fixed effects specifications can be severely biased in settings without untreated units, where identification relies entirely on within-treated variation. We illustrate the proposed framework through Monte Carlo simulations and two empirical applications, revisiting the effects of minimum wage policies and the consequences of hospitalization.

title: Homogeneity Without Legibility: Institutional Coordinates and Dynamic Closure

detail.title: Homogeneity Without Legibility: Institutional Coordinates and Dynamic Closure
detail.abstract: Institutions govern complex systems through reduced coordinates such as ratings, scores, and risk classes. This paper studies how consequential use changes the residual predictive error left after conditioning on a given coordinate. Idiosyncratic within-class variation can wash out in large populations, while omitted common variation survives aggregation. At high intensity, behavior can become completely homogeneous while closure error remains positive if the convergent position depends on a common state omitted by the coordinate. With multiple classes, limiting error is determined by which transition-relevant categories remain unpinned and by their population and transition weights; whether a category can be pinned is a property of rule design relative to the range of the omitted state, not of enforcement intensity. A Gaussian benchmark gives a simple hedge-ratio characterization of the finite-intensity path. Yet augmenting the information set by the omitted common state eliminates residual common uncertainty in the high-intensity limit. A ratings-based capital specialization derives the hidden component from an omitted systematic factor loading and maps institutional intensity to the effective bite of the regulatory constraint.

title: When Will the European Court of Human Rights Rule on the Right to Conscientious Objection to Military Service in Wartime?

detail.title: When Will the European Court of Human Rights Rule on the Right to Conscientious Objection to Military Service in Wartime?

declarations.funderStatement: The author is grateful to the Europe and Middle East Section of the Friends World Committee for Consultation (FWCC EMES) and the Peace Institute (Mirovni inštitut; Ljubljana, Slovenia) for support of the Research and Development (R&D) Work “Study of the problems, prospects and technologies of advancing national interests in protection of human right to conscientious objection to military service and involvement of conscientious objectors into alternative nonmilitary service, including the management of this service, for peaceful (nonviolent) defense of Ukraine, ensuring human security, national harmony and security, international peace and security” (the state registration number 0125U003717).

detail.abstract: This paper argues that next step in evolution of the case law of the European Court of Human Rights related to conscientious objection to military service, after the landmark judgments of Bayatyan v. Armenia [GC] and Mushfig Mammadov and Others v. Azerbaijan, might be a judgment related to conscientious objection in wartime. In the 2011 Bayatyan judgment the Court changed its case-law and found that the right to conscientious objection is protected by Article 9 of the European Convention on Human Rights. In Mushfig Mammadov judgment of 2019, related to conscription of a conscientious objector in the context of Azerbaijan’s armed conflict with Armenia over the Nagorno-Karabakh region, the Court found that a mere reference to the necessity of defending the territorial integrity of the State does not justify absence of an appropriate alternative nonmilitary service as substitution of military duty for conscientious objectors. A judgment related to conscientious objection in wartime might be passed after an application related to ongoing criminal punishments of conscientious objectors in Ukraine for their religious beliefs incompatible with military service, their arbitrary detentions and ill-treatment reported by the European Bureau for Conscientious Objection, along with inability of the Government to respect commitments regarding protection of right to conscientious objection taken in the context of Ukraine’s accession to the European Union.

title: Teaching Propensity Score Weighting with Published Open Data: An R Shiny Application Verified on Two Published Datasets
affiliations: Nanzan University

detail.title: Teaching Propensity Score Weighting with Published Open Data: An R Shiny Application Verified on Two Published Datasets

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. The study involves no human participants or new data collection. It reanalyses de-identified data already published as supporting information by the original authors, and uses the lalonde dataset distributed with the MatchIt package.
declarations.funderStatement: This work received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Propensity score weighting is now common in applied policy and health research, but the teaching materials available to researchers whose field is not statistics tend to stop at the estimate. This paper reports an R Shiny application that runs a single fixed route — propensity score, weights for the average treatment effect on the treated, covariate balance, common support, and a weighted logistic regression — and ends by producing the paragraphs in which that analysis would be reported. The estimand, the entry method and the balance statistics are fixed rather than offered as options, so that a learner follows one defensible specification through to a reportable sentence. The application was written after two course sessions had been drafted, and it implements what drafting them showed to be missing.

Two verifications are reported. The experimental benchmarks of the National Supported Work demonstration were recomputed from the deposited files, for earnings and for employment, in both circulating versions of the sample. The propensity scores deposited by Pitter et al. (2022) were then reproduced exactly, along with the residual deviance, the classification, and the two covariates the paper reports as differing between cohorts. Running the application on that second dataset exposed two defects in its own defaults, both invisible with the bundled example and both corrected before release. The course has not been taught and no learning outcomes are claimed.

title: From AI-Assisted Firms to Agentic Firms: A Theory of Organizational Creative Destruction in the Age of Autonomous Intelligence

detail.title: From AI-Assisted Firms to Agentic Firms: A Theory of Organizational Creative Destruction in the Age of Autonomous Intelligence
detail.abstract: Most economic analyses of artificial intelligence and employment model AI primarily as a technology adopted by incumbent firms. In this model, firms autonomously choose whether to automate tasks, reduce labor costs, and reallocate workers toward new tasks. Such a perspective captures an important component of technological change, but it may miss a distinct organizational mechanism that becomes possible when increasingly capable reasoning models are combined with autonomous agents. This paper develops a theory of organizational AI displacement. The central claim is that the economically disruptive unit of advanced AI may not be the automated task or the AI-augmented employee, but the AInative firm: a production organization in which a human principal, a small human team, or potentially no direct human operator coordinates a scalable population of AI agents that collectively perform research, planning, production, management, marketing, software development, and other business functions. Under sufficiently high agentic capability, the relevant competitive process is no longer simply firms adopt AI to reduce costs, but AI-native organizations compete with incumbent firms for market share. The distinction is theoretically important. Cost reduction within an incumbent firm need not destabilize organizational equilibria, particularly when labor costs constitute only one component of a firm s total competitive position. By contrast, an entrant that simultaneously combines lower organizational cost with superior or rapidly improving product quality can generate a qualitatively different form of competitive pressure. Once such firms acquire market share, scale effects, data, reputation, cash flow, and further computational resources may create positive feedback that accelerates displacement of incumbent firms. Incumbents then face a strategic choice between rapid organizational AI transformation and loss of market share. A formal model based on differentiated-product competition, replicator dynamics, and endogenous adoption is developed. The model yields acritical organizational advantage condition under which AI-native firms become an evolutionary threat to conventional firms even when incumbents themselves could technically adopt similar AI technologies. Thepaper further derives implications for labor demand, firm-size distributions, entry barriers, market concentration, taxation, and welfare institutions. The theory differs from task-based automation models by introducinginter -firm organizational displacement as a separate channel of labor-market transformation. It also differs from standard productivity narratives by treating AI capabilities as a source of new organizational forms rather thanmerely a factor-augmenting technology. The paper does not predict that mass unemployment is inevitable. Instead, it establishes conditions under which rapid AI capability growth can generate discontinuous organizational restructuring even when incumbent firms initially exhibit weak incentives toautomate.

title: Breaking the Taboo in Taboo Trade-Offs: A Multimodal, Multitask Framework for Discrete Choice Modelling
affiliations: , Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Health Policy & Management and Independent

detail.title: Breaking the Taboo in Taboo Trade-Offs: A Multimodal, Multitask Framework for Discrete Choice Modelling
detail.abstract: Healthcare policy routinely involves morally problematic, or taboo, trade-offs – such as lives for money or quality of life for efficiency. Individuals experience moral discomfort when confronted with such trade-offs, which is expressed as an aversion to trade sacred and secular outcomes. This behavior is known as taboo trade-off aversion (TTOA). Ignoring TTOA, when the behavior is present, misrepresents preferences and biases welfare estimates. Standard random utility maximization (RUM) models can accommodate TTOA by imposing theory-driven assumptions about which trade-offs are taboo. We introduce the taboo trade-off aversion neural network (TTOA-NN), a multimodal and multitask framework that identifies taboo trade-offs and individual aversion from data by combining stated-choice data with textual justifications. First, we conduct a simulation study to establish the framework’s identifiability properties. Then, we apply the new framework to an empirical study, a Dutch pandemic preparedness experiment, revealing deeper insights into which trade-offs are perceived as taboo. We find that TTOA is dominated by a single moral foundation – Authority – rather than by Care, Fairness, or Sanctity. This reveals that TTOA is rooted in deference to moral authority in the context of our application. The framework is modular, embeds into any RUM model, and reveals which trade-offs are taboo, who is averse to them, and to which moral orientation the aversion may be aligned with – grounded in the moral foundations people express in their own words. TTOA-NN enables policymakers to design interventions that respect moral constraints rather than violate them.

title: Insurance and Wealth as Determinants of Institutional Delivery Choice: Evidence from India

detail.title: Insurance and Wealth as Determinants of Institutional Delivery Choice: Evidence from India

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no personal or financial relationships that could have influenced or be perceived to have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study utilizes secondary, de-identified public data from the Fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019–21), conducted by the International Institute for Population Sciences (IIPS), Mumbai, under the aegis of the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare (MoHFW), Government of India. Ethical approval for the NFHS-5 survey protocol was granted by the IIPS Institutional Review Board and the ICF Institutional Review Board. Informed consent was obtained from all survey respondents prior to interview administration.
declarations.funderStatement: No external funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Evaluating how health insurance financing reshapes healthcare utilization and provides financial protection remains a central inquiry in health economics. We examine whether health insurance coverage influences the specific facility type in which women deliver-distinguishing between public health facilities, private health facilities, and home deliveries-rather than merely whether it increases generic institutional attendance. Utilizing nationally representative data from the Fifth National Family Health Survey (NFHS-5, 2019-21) covering 181,248 birth events in India, we address unobserved selection bias and endogeneity in health insurance enrollment using a Two-Stage Residual Inclusion (2SRI) multinomial logit model instrumented by mass media exposure. Our empirical estimates suggest that health insurance coverage significantly expands institutional childbirth, increasing public facility delivery likelihood by 4.2 percentage points (p < 0.01) and reducing home deliveries by 2.8 percentage points (p < 0.01), while lowering delivery out-of-pocket expenditure (OOPE) by 3.3% (approximately 376 INR per birth event).

title: Autolysis and Symbiosis - From Mythology to Distribution Economics - The Autolysis and Symbiosis of Civilization

detail.title: Autolysis and Symbiosis - From Mythology to Distribution Economics - The Autolysis and Symbiosis of Civilization

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.ethicsApproval: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: For the past five centuries, world history has largely been narrated in terms defined by Western civilization. Yet the very technologies that underwrote its modern hegemony — paper, gunpowder, and the compass — were invented in East Asia and transmitted westward. Beginning from this factual record, this paper examines the mythological substratum from which Western civilization grew, contrasting Hesiod’s Theogony with the Dangun myth of Korea. Where Western myth is structured around polemos () and patricidal succession — a narrative largely absent of humanity — πόλεμοςKorean myth centers on Hongik Ingan (弘益人間, “to broadly benefit humanity”) as the founding motive of creation, a narrative of humanity’s becoming. This paper argues that this mythological divergence produces two distinct modes of civilizational existence, synthesizing Arnold Toynbee’s thesis of civilizational suicide and the hubris–atē–nemesis structure of Greek tragedy under the concept of Jamyeol (私滅, autolysis), and grounding Gongsaeng (共生, symbiosis) ontologically in the Hwaeom Buddhist concept of sangjeuk-sangip (相卽相入, mutual interpenetration). It further diagnoses the clinical symptoms of autolysis — climate crisis, extreme polarization, and anomie — and proposes a Distribution Economics rooted in Korea’s traditional mutual-aid institutions (pumasi, dure, gye, hyangyak) as an alternative economic model for the post-scarcity age. Rather than borrowing the concept of Daedong (大同) from the Chinese Book of Rites, this paper proposes a genuinely Korean concept, Hwahap (火合, Pyrokoinonia — lit. “fire-communion,” from Greek and ),πῦρκοινωνία as the destination toward which the lineage from Hongik Ingan to Korea’s mutual-aid traditions has been moving. Drawing on Joseph Nye’s theory of soft power and Korea’s changed economic standing (its transition from an aid recipient to an aid donor nation, and its growth into a top-twelve global economy), this paper further argues that the material conditions are now in place for Distribution Economics to be broadcast as a global economic standard. The global enthusiasm for K-culture, it is argued, is a largely unconscious response to the fact that Gongsaeng civilization still retains a communal sensibility that autolytic civilization has lost. The paper concludes by proposing Distribution Economics not merely as a theoretical suggestion but as the future economic coordinate toward which Korea ought to orient itself.

title: Effort Under Threshold-Triggered Risk: A Stochastic Payoff Model and Its Game-Theoretic Implications

detail.title: Effort Under Threshold-Triggered Risk: A Stochastic Payoff Model and Its Game-Theoretic Implications
detail.abstract: Conventional models of effort and reward assume monotonicity of the relationship between the effort and payoffs, whereas in many economically interesting settings, effort beyond certain point introduces genuine uncertainty into the payoff, as opposed to simply making it larger. For example, overtraining in athletic or sports fields beyond a certain threshold which the human body can sustain leading to increased injury chances along with boosted performance. Many situations in finance where bidding more amounts come with a higher risk but also a possible huge return/profit. And many more real-life situations where exceeding some well known threshold might induce some jeopardy along with a prospective reward worth your risk. I propose a threshold-type stochastic payoff model, and study it from different angles. In the model, effort below a threshold leads to a conventional, deterministic payoff, whereas effort beyond the threshold leads to a gamble: either the effort is penalized by a "shock", or is boosted by a "gain", scaled-up by some factor related to the magnitude of the effort, is given, each with some probability, hence making the model a stochastic one. First, we examine the case of a single player maximizing the expected payoff. From our observations, we come to the conclusion that, for any single player, the optimal effort is to always exert the maximal effort possible, unless it has a constant absolute risk aversion utility function with coefficient high enough to offset the linear increase in the expected payoff from additional effort. Second, we characterize, again, for a single player case, a class of conditions (independent of any specific utility function) under which player will be "risk-averse" at a certain effort, i.e., there will be some effort above the mean-variance maximizing effort, such that any higher level of effort would lead to diminished payoffs to the player, with certainty. In particular, we derive that for any utility function whose constant absolute risk aversion is uniformly bounded below by a positive constant, and for any symmetric effort-payoff-gain specification, such danger point threshold is given by a universal constant ln 2 , in the limit of wide effort range. Finally, we examine a symmetric winner-take-all two-player game, and show that, in the absence of direct cost of effort, the game has a unique Nash equilibrium at maximal effort of both players, irrespective of any set of parameter values for which it is well-defined, contrary to the intuition from the single-agent case, in which the same payoff structure leads to risk-aversion for any player with constant absolute risk aversion utility function. Introducing a convex cost of effort allows the game to have an interior Nash equilibrium, however, for intermediate values of this cost parameter, there are no pure strategy equilibrium in the game, which is similar to the result for all-pay auctions. In particular, our result illustrates that competition can cause the players to be less rationally risk averse than they would be otherwise, thus pushing the effort levels to the very edge of the domain, even when they are individually sub-optimal. This paper takes three individual research points, the single player game simulation, the closed form algebraic formulation and the two player game monte-carlo simulation to observe, analyze and connect the three situations to study, infer and try to mimic some real life escalating situations as closely as possible.

title: Multi-Stage Neural Networks with Learnable Intermediate Bridges: From a Theoretical Framework to Production Retrieval-Augmented Generation

detail.title: Multi-Stage Neural Networks with Learnable Intermediate Bridges: From a Theoretical Framework to Production Retrieval-Augmented Generation
detail.abstract: In 2018 we formalized a framework for compositional systems of three neural networks connected by learnable intermediate bridges-trainable interface modules governed by explicit contracts on shape, semantics, distributional stability, information content, and computational budget (Bergo, 2018). The central hypothesis was that structured decomposition with explicit interface contracts can outperform monolithic scaling whenever a task naturally separates into perception, inference, and generation stages. This article revisits that framework in light of a 2025 production deployment: a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) system in which a budget-constrained reranking "sidecar" realizes the perception-inference bridge and a QLoRA adapter (Dettmers et al., 2023) realizes the inference-generation bridge. In internal production evaluation, the deployed system exhibited no detected hallucinations on its evaluation suite, sustained a sidecar latency below 0.3 ms, and reduced generator input tokens by more than 90% relative to conventional RAG. We present the mathematical foundation, a taxonomy of bridge modules, the training methodology, an event-driven execution model, and an information-theoretic analysis-grounded in the information bottleneck principle (Tishby et al., 2000)-of why bridge-mediated context compression structurally suppresses hallucination. We argue that the interface between models, rather than the models themselves, is the primary design object for reliable multi-stage systems.

title: Psychological Counseling in the World of Work

detail.title: Psychological Counseling in the World of Work

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is President of the Verband Psychologischer Berater e.V. (VpsyB), Lead Lecturer at the Akademie Psychologischer Berater, and Honorary Professor of Counseling Psychology. She therefore represents institutional interests in the field of non-medical psychological counseling; the initiative mentioned in this paper is co-sponsored by VpsyB e.V. The paper is intended as a scientific assessment of the field; the roles stated above are disclosed in the interest of transparency. No third party funding was received for its preparation. To the author's knowledge, there are no other financial or personal conflicts of interest.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper does not involve any studies with human participants or animals. It is based exclusively on the analysis of publicly available data, legal sources, and scientific literature. Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: No external or third-party funding was received for this research. The work was self-funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
The world of work is one of the central settings in which mental strain arises, becomes visible, and generates economic costs in Germany. Absence days attributable to mental disorders continue to reach new record levels, and mental disorders are among the most common causes of early retirement. The demands of Work 4.0 and New Work—digitalization, the blurring of boundaries, acceleration, and increasing complexity—further intensify this strain.

This paper argues that this development can be addressed neither by treatment within the scope of the legally defined practice of medicine and healing (Heilkunde) nor by structural occupational safety measures alone. Rather, individual primary prevention is required that intervenes before strain develops into disorders requiring treatment. Non-medical psychological counseling is described as a low-threshold, resource-oriented, confidential service that is clearly delineated from the practice of medicine and healing and can close this gap.

This paper was originally written in German by the author. AI-assisted translation tool (Open AI) was used solely for a literal, word-for-word translation into English, without any content changes. The author reviewed and verified the translated text for accuracy.
